subject: sci
title: Chemistry: Matter, Atoms, Reactions, Solutions, and pH
objectives: You will describe solids, liquids, and gases and the phase changes between them in terms of particle motion, and read a heating curve.
You will use atomic number and mass number to find the protons, neutrons, and electrons in an atom, and use the periodic table to predict which elements behave alike.
You will classify matter as elements, compounds, or mixtures and classify changes as physical or chemical using evidence.
You will balance chemical equations and apply the law of conservation of mass to lab data from open and sealed containers.
You will calculate density and concentration, read solubility tables and graphs, and interpret the pH scale.

slides.title: Chemistry: Matter, Atoms, Reactions, Solutions, and pH
slides.board:
Today you will:

  • Explain states of matter and phase changes with particles
  • Count protons, neutrons, and electrons; read the periodic table
  • Classify matter and changes
  • Balance equations and use conservation of mass
  • Calculate density and concentration; read solubility and pH

Plan: Warm-up → 7 big ideas → practice together → your turn → GED-style questions

notes.say: Welcome to Week 7 of Science: chemistry. Chemistry sounds intimidating, but on the GED it comes down to a handful of rules you apply to a table, a graph, or a short lab story. Today we learn those rules one at a time and practice each one right away. The three that earn the most points are balancing equations, conservation of mass, and reading data on density, solubility, and pH, so we will spend the most time there.
ask: What comes to mind when you hear the word 'chemistry'? (expected answer: any answer; point out that cooking, cleaning, rust, and burning fuel are all chemistry they already know)

slides.title: Warm-Up: Ecosystems Review
slides.board:
1. Food chain: grass → grasshopper → frog → snake. Which organism is the secondary consumer?
  2. The producers store 20,000 kcal. About how much energy reaches the secondary consumers?
  3. Which process removes carbon dioxide from the air?
  4. Green and brown beetles live on brown bark. Birds spot green beetles more easily. After many generations, which color is more common, and why?
steps: 1. The frog. Grass is the producer, the grasshopper is the primary consumer, and the frog eats the grasshopper.
2. Two steps up at about 10% each: 20,000 × 0.10 = 2,000; 2,000 × 0.10 = 200 kcal.
3. Photosynthesis. Plants take in CO2 and use it to make sugar. (Oceans also absorb CO2.)
4. Brown. Brown beetles survive and reproduce more, so the inherited brown trait becomes more common. That is natural selection.

notes.say: These review last week's ecosystems lesson, and two of them lead straight into today. The carbon cycle is chemistry: burning, respiration, and photosynthesis are chemical reactions, and matter cycles because atoms are never created or destroyed. Give the student about three minutes, then have them tell you each answer before you reveal it.
ask: Last week we said matter cycles but energy does not. What does it mean for matter to cycle? (expected answer: the same atoms are used again and again; they are not used up)
notes.answer: 1. Frog. 2. 200 kcal. 3. Photosynthesis (ocean absorption also counts). 4. Brown, because brown beetles are eaten less, survive, and pass the brown trait to more offspring.
notes.watch: On question 2, students often multiply by 0.10 only once (2,000 kcal) or count organisms instead of arrows. Have them point to each arrow and multiply once per arrow.

slides.title: Big Idea 1: States of Matter and Phase Changes
slides.board:
StateShapeVolumeParticles
SolidFixedFixedPacked tight, vibrate in place
LiquidTakes container'sFixedClose, slide past each other
GasFills containerFills containerFar apart, fast

Add heat: melt, evaporate/boil, sublime (solid → gas). Remove heat: freeze, condense.

During a phase change, temperature stays flat.

notes.say: Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space, and all of it is made of particles that never stop moving. What makes something a solid, liquid, or gas is how fast its particles move and how close together they are. Adding heat speeds the particles up until they break free into the next state; removing heat does the reverse. Look at the graph: while ice melts and while water boils, the line goes flat. The heat is being used to pull particles apart, not to make them move faster, so the temperature does not rise until the change is finished.
ask: Why does a gas fill its whole container? (expected answer: its particles are far apart and move fast in all directions until they hit the walls)
Dry ice turns straight into a gas. What is that called? (expected answer: sublimation)
notes.watch: Students often think the temperature keeps climbing while water boils. Point to the flat part of the graph and ask what the thermometer reads the whole time water is boiling: 100 °C at sea level.

slides.title: Worked Example: Read a Heating Curve
slides.board:
Use the heating curve of water.

  1. At what temperature does the ice melt?
  2. How many minutes does the boiling last?
  3. What state is the water in from 6 to 14 minutes?
  4. Why is the line flat from 14 to 20 minutes?
steps: 1. The first flat part is melting. It sits at 0 °C.
2. The second flat part (boiling) runs from 14 to 20 minutes: 20 − 14 = 6 minutes.
3. Between the two flat parts, all the ice has melted and none has boiled yet: liquid.
4. The heat is pulling liquid particles apart into gas instead of speeding them up, so the temperature stays at 100 °C until all the water has boiled.

notes.say: Here is how I read any heating curve. Rising parts mean one state is warming up. Flat parts mean a phase change: the lower flat part is melting or freezing, and the higher flat part is boiling or condensing. To find how long something takes, subtract the start time from the end time on the x-axis; to find a temperature, read across to the y-axis.
ask: What is happening from 0 to 2 minutes? (expected answer: solid ice is warming from −20 °C to 0 °C)
notes.watch: A common slip is reading the time axis when the question asks for temperature, or the reverse. Have the student put a finger on the axis named in the question before answering.

notes.say: Every element is built from atoms, and every atom has the same three parts. Protons and neutrons sit in the tiny center called the nucleus; electrons move around it. The number of protons is the atom's ID card: change it and you have a different element. That is the atomic number. Add the neutrons and you get the mass number, because electrons are so light they barely count. In the picture, lithium-7 has 3 protons and 4 neutrons, so its mass number is 7, and as a neutral atom it has 3 electrons.
ask: Carbon-14 has atomic number 6. How many neutrons? (expected answer: 14 − 6 = 8)
If an atom gains an electron, is it still the same element? (expected answer: yes; only the proton count names the element; it becomes a negative ion)
notes.watch: The most common error is using the mass number as the number of protons. Have students write "p = atomic number" at the top of their scratch paper every time.

slides.title: The Periodic Table: Columns Behave Alike
slides.board:
• Elements are in order of atomic number.
  • Rows = periods. Columns = groups.
  • Same group = same number of outer electrons = similar properties.
  • Metals on the left; nonmetals on the right.
Group 1Group 17Group 18
Li, Na, KF, Cl, BrHe, Ne, Ar
Soft metals; react strongly with waterReactive nonmetalsNoble gases; rarely react

notes.say: The periodic table is not just a list; its layout predicts behavior. Elements in the same column have the same number of outer electrons, and those outer electrons decide how an atom reacts. So if the GED tells you that sodium reacts violently with water and asks which other element would act the same way, look straight down the column: potassium. The far-right column, the noble gases, almost never react, which is why helium is safe in balloons.
ask: Bromine is in the same group as chlorine. Predict one property of bromine. (expected answer: it is a reactive nonmetal, like chlorine)
Why would you expect neon to be unreactive? (expected answer: it is in Group 18, the noble gases)
notes.watch: Some students pick the element in the same row because it is "next to" the given element. Remind them: rows change properties; columns share them.

slides.title: Worked Example: Count the Particles
slides.board:
A potassium atom has atomic number 19 and mass number 39.

  1. How many protons, neutrons, and electrons does a neutral potassium atom have?
  2. Potassium is in Group 1 with sodium. Predict how potassium reacts with water.
steps: Protons = atomic number = 19.
Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 39 − 19 = 20.
Neutral atom, so electrons = protons = 19.
Same group as sodium, so potassium reacts strongly with water, just as sodium does (in fact, even more strongly).

notes.say: I always go in the same order: protons from the atomic number, neutrons by subtracting, electrons equal to protons if the atom is neutral. Then for the prediction I do not need to memorize anything about potassium; I only need to know that it shares a column with sodium.
ask: What would change if this potassium atom lost one electron? (expected answer: it would have 18 electrons and a +1 charge; it would be a potassium ion, still potassium)

slides.title: We Do: Atoms and States
slides.board:
1. Oxygen: atomic number 8, mass number 16. Find protons, neutrons, and electrons.
  2. An atom has 26 protons and 30 neutrons. What is its mass number?
  3. Which element behaves most like fluorine: oxygen, chlorine, or neon?
  4. A puddle disappears on a warm day. Name the phase change and explain it with particles.
steps: 1. Protons 8; neutrons 16 − 8 = 8; electrons 8.
2. 26 + 30 = 56. (This is iron-56; 26 protons makes it iron.)
3. Chlorine: it is in the same group (Group 17) as fluorine. Oxygen and neon are only neighbors in the same row.
4. Evaporation (liquid → gas). The water particles gain energy from the warm air and sun, move faster, and escape the liquid as gas.

notes.say: Let's do these together. You talk me through each step, and I will reveal it after you commit. On number 3, say out loud whether you are looking at the row or the column.
ask: On number 2, how did you know the element is iron? (expected answer: 26 protons; the atomic number of iron is 26)
notes.answer: 1. 8 protons, 8 neutrons, 8 electrons. 2. 56. 3. Chlorine (same group). 4. Evaporation: particles gain energy and escape as a gas.
notes.watch: On number 2, students sometimes subtract (30 − 26 = 4). Ask: "Mass number counts everything in the nucleus. Do we add or subtract?"

slides.title: Big Idea 3: Kinds of Matter and Kinds of Change
slides.board:
ElementCompoundMixture
One kind of atom: Fe, O2Elements bonded in a fixed ratio: H2O, NaClNot bonded, any ratio: salt water, air

Physical change: same substance (melt, cut, dissolve, boil).

Chemical change: new substance. Clues: gas bubbles, color change, heat or light, a new solid (precipitate), new odor.

H2O: the subscript 2 = two H atoms; no number = one O.

notes.say: Everything around you is an element, a compound, or a mixture. A compound is not just stuck together; its atoms are chemically bonded, and its properties can be completely different from its elements. Sodium is a metal that explodes in water and chlorine is a poison gas, yet bonded together they make table salt. A mixture, like salt water, can be separated by physical means such as evaporation or filtering. Changes work the same way: a physical change keeps the same substance, while a chemical change makes a new one, and the GED expects you to name the evidence.
ask: Is dissolving sugar in tea a chemical change? (expected answer: no; it is still sugar, and you could get it back by evaporating the water)
How many atoms of each element are in CO<sub>2</sub>? (expected answer: 1 carbon, 2 oxygen)
notes.watch: Students often call dissolving or boiling a chemical change because something seems to disappear. Ask: "Is it still the same substance?" Boiled water is still water.

slides.title: Worked Example: Classify It
slides.board:
Classify each one.

  1. Is carbon dioxide (CO2) an element, a compound, or a mixture?
  2. Is air an element, a compound, or a mixture?
  3. A tablet dropped in water fizzes and gives off a gas. Physical or chemical change?
  4. Ice cream melts on a hot day. Physical or chemical change?
steps: 1. Two different elements (C and O) bonded in a fixed 1 : 2 ratio: a compound.
2. Nitrogen, oxygen, and other gases mixed together, not bonded, and the amounts vary: a mixture.
3. A new gas forms: chemical change.
4. It changes state but is still ice cream: physical change.

notes.say: For matter, I ask two questions: how many kinds of atoms, and are they bonded? One kind is an element. More than one kind, bonded in a fixed formula, is a compound. Not bonded is a mixture. For changes, I ask one question: is there a new substance? Then I look for the evidence.
ask: Is oxygen gas, O<sub>2</sub>, an element or a compound? It has two atoms. (expected answer: an element; both atoms are oxygen)
notes.watch: O2, N2, and H2 trip students up: two atoms does not mean compound. A compound needs two or more different elements.

slides.title: Your Turn: Atoms, Matter, and Changes
slides.board:
1. Chlorine: atomic number 17, mass number 35. Neutrons? Electrons in a neutral atom?
  2. Element, compound, or mixture: (a) gold, (b) table salt, NaCl, (c) trail mix.
  3. Physical or chemical: (a) an iron gate rusts, (b) a glass bottle shatters, (c) milk sours.
  4. Which state has a fixed volume but no fixed shape?
steps: 1. Neutrons 35 − 17 = 18; electrons 17.
2. (a) element, (b) compound, (c) mixture.
3. (a) chemical (new substance, rust), (b) physical (still glass), (c) chemical (new sour-tasting acid forms).
4. Liquid.

notes.say: Work these alone; you have four minutes. Tell me your answers when you are done, and for number 3, tell me the evidence you used. I will reveal only after you commit.
notes.answer: 1. 18 neutrons, 17 electrons. 2. (a) element, (b) compound, (c) mixture. 3. (a) chemical, (b) physical, (c) chemical. 4. Liquid.
notes.watch: On 3(b), some students say chemical because the bottle cannot be put back together. "Cannot undo" is not the test; "new substance" is. Broken glass is still glass.

slides.title: Big Idea 4: Equations and Conservation of Mass
slides.board:
Reactants → Products

Conservation of mass: atoms are rearranged, never created or destroyed. Mass of reactants = mass of products.

To balance:

  1. Count each atom on both sides.
  2. Change only coefficients (big front numbers). Never subscripts.
  3. Coefficient × subscript = atoms: 3H2O has 6 H and 3 O.
  4. Save H, O, and lone elements for last. Recount.

notes.say: A chemical equation is a recipe: reactants on the left, products on the right. The law of conservation of mass says the same atoms that go in must come out, just rearranged, so the total mass before equals the total mass after. That is why we balance equations. We are allowed to change only the coefficients, the numbers in front, because changing a subscript changes the substance itself: H<sub>2</sub>O is water, but H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> is hydrogen peroxide.
ask: How many oxygen atoms are in 2CO<sub>2</sub>? (expected answer: 2 × 2 = 4)
If 12 g of reactants react completely, what mass of products forms? (expected answer: 12 g)
notes.watch: Students forget that a coefficient multiplies every atom in the formula. Have them write the multiplication out: 2H2O → H: 2 × 2 = 4; O: 2 × 1 = 2.

slides.title: Worked Example: Balance Burning Natural Gas
slides.board:
Balance: CH4 + O2 → CO2 + H2O

AtomLeftRight
C11
H42
O23
steps: Carbon: 1 and 1. Already balanced.
Hydrogen: 4 on the left, 2 on the right. Write 2H2O: now 2 × 2 = 4 H.
Oxygen: right side is now 2 (in CO2) + 2 (in 2H2O) = 4. Left has 2. Write 2O2: 2 × 2 = 4.
Recount: C 1 = 1, H 4 = 4, O 4 = 4. CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O

notes.say: I always make an atom chart first; it takes twenty seconds and prevents most mistakes. Carbon appears in only one substance on each side, so I check it first. Then hydrogen. I save oxygen for last because O<sub>2</sub> is a lone element and I can adjust it without disturbing anything else. After every change, I update the chart.
ask: After writing 2H<sub>2</sub>O, why did the oxygen count on the right change? (expected answer: the 2 multiplies the oxygen in water too: 2 × 1 = 2 more O)
notes.watch: Watch for students who write CH4 + O4 or H4O2. That is changing subscripts. Cross it out and go back to coefficients.

slides.title: Worked Example: Balance Rust (the LCM Move)
slides.board:
Balance: Fe + O2 → Fe2O3

Left: Fe 1, O 2.   Right: Fe 2, O 3.

Oxygen comes in 2s on one side and 3s on the other.
steps: Find the smallest number both 2 and 3 divide into: 6.
Left: 3O2 gives 3 × 2 = 6 O. Right: 2Fe2O3 gives 2 × 3 = 6 O.
Iron: the right now has 2 × 2 = 4 Fe, so write 4Fe on the left.
Recount: Fe 4 = 4, O 6 = 6. 4Fe + 3O2 → 2Fe2O3

notes.say: When one side has an even number of an atom and the other side an odd number, use the least common multiple. Oxygen here is 2 versus 3, so I aim for 6 on both sides. Once oxygen is fixed, iron follows. The GED often gives these as drop-down menus in front of each formula, so practice choosing all three numbers before checking.
ask: A student writes 2Fe + O<sub>2</sub> → Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>. What is still wrong? (expected answer: oxygen: 2 on the left, 3 on the right)

slides.title: We Do: The Propane Grill
slides.board:
A grill burns propane: C3H8 + O2 → CO2 + H2O

  1. Balance the equation.
  2. Physical or chemical change? Give two pieces of evidence.
  3. 44 g of propane reacts completely with 160 g of oxygen. What is the total mass of the products?
steps: 1. Carbon: 3 on the left, so 3CO2. Hydrogen: 8 on the left, so 4H2O (4 × 2 = 8).
Oxygen on the right: 3 × 2 + 4 × 1 = 6 + 4 = 10, so 5O2. C3H8 + 5O2 → 3CO2 + 4H2O (C 3 = 3, H 8 = 8, O 10 = 10).
2. Chemical: new substances (CO2 and water) form, and heat and light are given off.
3. Conservation of mass: 44 g + 160 g = 204 g of products.

notes.say: Let's do this one together. Same order as before: carbon, then hydrogen, oxygen last. Tell me each coefficient before I reveal it. For question 3, notice that you do not need any chemistry beyond one rule: what goes in comes out.
ask: Where did the 10 oxygen atoms on the right come from? (expected answer: 3 × 2 from carbon dioxide plus 4 × 1 from water)
notes.answer: 1. C3H8 + 5O2 → 3CO2 + 4H2O. 2. Chemical; new substances form and heat and light are released. 3. 204 g.
notes.watch: When counting oxygen on the right, students often forget the oxygen in water and write 3O2. Have them circle every O on the right before adding.

slides.title: Your Turn: Balance and Weigh
slides.board:
1. Balance: Mg + O2 → MgO
  2. Balance: N2 + H2 → NH3
  3. A candle burns on a scale in an open room, and the reading drops by 3 g. Was mass destroyed?
  4. Steel wool weighing 10.0 g is burned in an open dish. Afterward it weighs 10.6 g. Where did the extra 0.6 g come from?
steps: 1. 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO (Mg 2 = 2, O 2 = 2).
2. N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3 (N 2 = 2, H 6 = 6).
3. No. The wax becomes carbon dioxide and water vapor, which are gases that drift away unweighed.
4. Oxygen from the air combined with the iron to make iron oxide. The oxygen was never weighed at the start.

notes.say: Four minutes, on your own. Problems 3 and 4 are mirror images: in one the mass goes down and in the other it goes up, but the explanation is the same. Ask yourself what gas left or what gas joined from the air.
notes.answer: 1. 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO. 2. N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3. 3. No; gaseous products escaped the open room's scale. 4. Oxygen from the air combined with the iron; total mass is still conserved.
notes.watch: For problem 4, some students say mass was created. Ask: "Was the oxygen on the scale at the start?" Conservation of mass holds only when you count everything that reacts.

slides.title: Big Idea 5: Density
slides.board:
Density = mass ÷ volume   (D = m ÷ V)

Units: g/mL or g/cm3 (1 mL = 1 cm3)

  • Water = 1.00 g/mL. Less dense floats; more dense sinks.
  • Density identifies a substance: same substance, same density, any size.
  • Water displacement: volume = final level − starting level.

notes.say: Density tells you how tightly matter is packed. A pound of feathers and a pound of lead have the same mass, but the lead takes up far less space, so it is denser. Density is a property of the substance, not the object: a gold ring and a gold bar have the same density. That is why we can use it to identify an unknown metal. For a lump with an odd shape, drop it in water; the rise in the water level is its volume.
ask: A block has a density of 0.8 g/cm<sup>3</sup>. Will it float in water? (expected answer: yes, 0.8 < 1.00)
If you cut that block in half, what is the density of each half? (expected answer: still 0.8 g/cm<sup>3</sup>)
notes.watch: Students sometimes divide volume by mass. Anchor it in the units: grams per milliliter means grams on top.

ask: What would the density be if the bolt were twice as large? (expected answer: the same, 7.87 g/cm<sup>3</sup>; mass and volume both double)

slides.title: Big Idea 6: Solutions, Concentration, and Solubility
slides.board:
Solute (what dissolves) + solvent (does the dissolving) = solution

Concentration (g/L) = grams of solute ÷ liters of solution

  • Adding water dilutes: same solute, more volume, lower concentration.
  • Solubility = most solute that can dissolve at a given temperature. At that limit: saturated.
  • Most solids: more soluble when warmer. Gases: less soluble when warmer.

notes.say: A solution is an even mixture, like sugar in tea. Concentration tells you how much solute is packed into the solution, and the most common unit on the GED is grams per liter, so always convert milliliters to liters first. Solubility is the limit: the most that can dissolve at a certain temperature. On this graph you can see that potassium nitrate's limit climbs steeply as the water warms, while sodium chloride barely changes. Gases are the opposite of most solids, which is why a warm soda goes flat.
ask: How much potassium nitrate can dissolve in 100 g of water at 40 °C? (expected answer: 64 g)
You add water to a cup of salt water. What happens to the amount of salt? To the concentration? (expected answer: the salt stays the same; the concentration goes down)
notes.watch: Forgetting to convert mL to L is the top error: 24 g in 400 mL is 24 ÷ 0.400 = 60 g/L, not 0.06 g/L.

slides.title: Worked Example: Crystals from a Cooling Solution
slides.board:
Potassium chloride: about 51 g dissolves per 100 g water at 80 °C, and about 34 g at 20 °C.

A student dissolves 50 g of potassium chloride in 100 g of water at 80 °C, then cools it to 20 °C. How many grams of solid come out of solution?
steps: At 80 °C: 50 g < 51 g, so all 50 g dissolves (unsaturated).
At 20 °C: only 34 g can stay dissolved.
Solid that comes out = 50 g − 34 g = 16 g.
Trap: 51 − 34 = 17 g would be right only if the solution had been saturated (51 g) at 80 °C.

notes.say: Always start from the amount actually dissolved, not from the solubility limit. First I check that everything dissolved at the high temperature. Then I find the new limit at the low temperature. Whatever is above the new limit has to come out as crystals.
ask: What if the student had dissolved only 30 g? (expected answer: no crystals; 30 g is below the 34 g limit at 20 °C)

slides.title: Big Idea 7: Acids, Bases, and pH
slides.board:
pH0–6.977.1–14
TypeAcid (sour)NeutralBase (bitter, slippery)

Each 1 pH unit = 10 times.
2 units = 100×   3 units = 1,000×

Lower pH = more acidic. Acid + base → neutralize (pH moves toward 7).

notes.say: The pH scale runs from 0 to 14. Below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral like pure water, and above 7 is basic. The one fact the GED tests most often is that the scale counts by powers of 10. Each step of 1 is ten times; two steps is ten times ten, a hundred; three steps is a thousand. So lemon juice at pH 2 is not a little more acidic than vinegar at pH 3; it is ten times more acidic.
ask: Ammonia has pH 11. Acid or base? (expected answer: base)
Which is more acidic, pH 3 or pH 5, and by how much? (expected answer: pH 3, by 100 times)
notes.watch: Students often subtract and stop ("2 times") or multiply the difference by 10 ("20 times"). Have them write 10 once for each unit of difference and multiply: 10 × 10 = 100.

slides.title: Worked Example: How Many Times More Acidic?
slides.board:
Rainwater in one town has pH 4. A nearby lake has pH 7.

  1. Is the rainwater acidic, neutral, or basic?
  2. How many times more acidic is the rainwater than the lake?
steps: 1. 4 is below 7: acidic.
2. Difference: 7 − 4 = 3 units.
Each unit is ×10: 10 × 10 × 10 = 103 = 1,000 times more acidic.
Traps: 3 times (just the difference) and 30 times (difference × 10) both ignore the powers of 10.

notes.say: Two moves every time: subtract the pH values to get the number of steps, then write that many tens and multiply. Three steps means ten to the third, one thousand. Notice the lower pH is the more acidic one, so the rain is the more acidic sample.
ask: How many times more basic is pH 12 than pH 10? (expected answer: 100 times)

slides.title: We Do: Density, Concentration, and pH
slides.board:
1. A stone has a mass of 63 g. The water level rises from 30 mL to 51 mL. Find its density. Float or sink?
  2. A sports drink has 24 g of sugar in 400 mL. Find the concentration in g/L.
  3. 200 mL of a 30 g/L salt solution gets 100 mL of water added. New concentration?
  4. Black coffee is pH 5; milk is pH 6. Which is more acidic, and by what factor?
steps: 1. V = 51 − 30 = 21 mL. D = 63 ÷ 21 = 3 g/mL. 3 > 1.00, so it sinks.
2. 400 mL = 0.400 L. 24 ÷ 0.400 = 60 g/L.
3. Salt: 0.200 L × 30 g/L = 6 g. New volume 0.300 L. 6 ÷ 0.300 = 20 g/L.
4. Coffee, by 10 times (one unit).

notes.say: We will do these together, one at a time. For each one, tell me the formula first, then the numbers. Number 3 is the dilution trap: the salt does not change, only the volume does.
ask: On number 3, why can't the answer be higher than 30 g/L? (expected answer: adding water only spreads the same salt into more liquid, so the concentration must go down)
notes.answer: 1. 3 g/mL; sinks. 2. 60 g/L. 3. 20 g/L. 4. Coffee, 10 times more acidic.
notes.watch: On number 3, students often answer 15 g/L (thinking the volume doubled) or keep 30 g/L. Have them find the grams of salt first.

slides.title: Your Turn: Numbers in Chemistry
slides.board:
1. A plastic block: mass 30 g, volume 40 cm3. Density? Float or sink?
  2. A nurse dissolves 18 g of salt to make 2.0 L of solution. Concentration?
  3. Solution A is pH 2; Solution B is pH 5. Which is more acidic, and by what factor?
  4. Potassium nitrate: 110 g dissolves per 100 g water at 60 °C and 32 g at 20 °C. You dissolve 100 g at 60 °C and cool to 20 °C. Grams of crystals?
steps: 1. 30 ÷ 40 = 0.75 g/cm3; 0.75 < 1.00, so it floats.
2. 18 ÷ 2.0 = 9 g/L.
3. Solution A, by 103 = 1,000 times.
4. All 100 g dissolves (100 < 110). 100 − 32 = 68 g.

notes.say: Five minutes on your own. Write the formula before you put in numbers. When you are done, tell me each answer with its unit.
notes.answer: 1. 0.75 g/cm3; floats. 2. 9 g/L. 3. Solution A, 1,000 times. 4. 68 g.
notes.watch: On number 4, watch for 78 g (110 − 32). Ask: "How much did you actually dissolve?"

slides.title: GED-Style Question: The Disappearing Mass
slides.board:
A student places a flask of vinegar and a cup of baking soda on a balance: 182.40 g. She pours the baking soda into the open flask. It fizzes. Afterward, the flask and empty cup weigh 181.30 g.

Which statement best explains the change in mass?

A. 1.10 g of matter was destroyed when the reaction released energy.
B. Carbon dioxide gas formed and escaped from the open flask.
C. The baking soda dissolved, which is a physical change that lowers mass.
D. The products of a reaction always have less mass than the reactants.
steps: A is out. Matter is never destroyed in a chemical reaction. That is the law of conservation of mass.
C is out. The fizzing shows a new gas formed, which is a chemical change. And dissolving does not change mass either.
D is out. Products always have the same total mass as the reactants when everything is counted.
B is correct. The fizzing was CO2 gas. In an open flask it escaped into the room, so the balance did not weigh it: 182.40 − 181.30 = 1.10 g of gas.

notes.say: Every wrong choice here breaks the law of conservation of mass in a different way. On the GED, when mass seems to disappear or appear, look for a gas and an open container. Read the stem, find the fizzing, and you have the answer before you read the choices.
ask: How could the student change the setup to show that mass is conserved? (expected answer: seal the container, for example a capped bottle, so the gas stays inside and is weighed)
notes.answer: B. Carbon dioxide gas escaped from the open flask; its mass, 1.10 g, was not weighed afterward. In a sealed container, the mass would stay at 182.40 g.

slides.title: GED-Style Question: Read the Solubility Graph
slides.board:
Use the solubility graph. A student has 100 g of water at 40 °C and adds 50 g of potassium chloride while stirring.

Which best describes the result?

A. All 50 g dissolves, because potassium chloride's solubility rises as temperature rises.
B. All 50 g dissolves, because 50 g is less than potassium nitrate's 64 g at 40 °C.
C. About 40 g dissolves and about 10 g stays solid; the solution is saturated.
D. About 10 g dissolves and about 40 g stays solid; the solution is unsaturated.
steps: Read the graph first: potassium chloride at 40 °C is about 40 g per 100 g water.
A is out. Solubility does rise with temperature, but at 40 °C the limit is 40 g, less than 50 g.
B is out. It reads the wrong line (potassium nitrate).
D is out. It flips the amounts, and a solution with extra solid sitting undissolved is saturated, not unsaturated.
C is correct. 40 g dissolves (the limit); 50 − 40 = 10 g stays solid; a solution at its limit is saturated.

notes.say: Graph questions on the GED often have a choice that reads the wrong line, so put your finger on the right line and the right temperature before you read the choices. Then compare: is the amount added more or less than the limit? More than the limit means some stays solid and the solution is saturated.
ask: What could the student do to dissolve all 50 g? (expected answer: heat the water to about 80 °C, where the limit is about 51 g, or add more water)
notes.answer: C. At 40 °C the limit is about 40 g per 100 g water, so 40 g dissolves, 10 g stays solid, and the solution is saturated.
notes.watch: If the student picks B, they read potassium nitrate. Have them trace the legend color to the potassium chloride line.

slides.title: Test Strategy: Chart It, Then Calculate
slides.board:
• Balancing: make an atom chart (element | left | right). Update it after every coefficient.
  • Formulas: write the formula with words first: D = m ÷ V; g/L = g ÷ L.
  • Units: mL → L before g/L. Volume by displacement = change in level.
  • pH: difference → that many 10s multiplied.
  • Mass changed? Look for a gas and an open container.

Use the on-screen calculator for every division.

notes.say: The GED Science test gives you a calculator on screen, so the arithmetic is not the hard part; the setup is. Every chemistry calculation has one formula and one trap. Write the formula in words on your scratch paper, put the numbers in, and check the unit. For balancing, the atom chart takes less than a minute and catches the most common error: forgetting that a coefficient multiplies every atom in a formula.
ask: What two things should you look for when a question says the mass went down? (expected answer: a gas product and an open container)

slides.title: Recap and What Comes Next
slides.board:
1. Heat speeds particles; phase changes happen at flat parts of a heating curve.
  2. Protons = atomic number; neutrons = mass number − atomic number. Same column, similar behavior.
  3. Chemical change = new substance. Balance with coefficients only; mass in = mass out.
  4. Density = m ÷ V; concentration = g ÷ L; crystals = amount dissolved − new limit.
  5. Each pH unit = 10 times.

Then do Practice Set A; if you score under 80 percent, take Set B. Finish with the Exit Check, where you need 6 of 8.
ask: How many neutrons does an atom with atomic number 13 and mass number 27 have? (expected answer: 14)
Why can't you balance an equation by changing a subscript? (expected answer: it changes the substance)
pH 3 versus pH 6: how many times more acidic? (expected answer: 1,000 times)

screens.title: What you will learn
screens.html:
Chemistry is the study of matter and how it changes. On the GED Science test, chemistry questions usually give you a short lab description, a table, or a graph and ask you to apply a few key rules. You do not need to memorize the periodic table. In this lesson you will learn to:

  • Explain solids, liquids, and gases and phase changes using particles, and read a heating curve.
  • Find the protons, neutrons, and electrons in an atom and use the periodic table to predict which elements act alike.
  • Classify matter as an element, compound, or mixture, and changes as physical or chemical.
  • Balance chemical equations and use the law of conservation of mass.
  • Calculate density and concentration, read solubility data, and use the pH scale.

Each screen teaches one idea and ends with a quick check. Keep scratch paper and a calculator nearby.

screens.title: States of matter
screens.html:
Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space. All matter is made of tiny particles that are always moving. The state of matter depends on how fast the particles move and how close together they are.

StateShapeVolumeParticles
SolidDefiniteDefinitePacked tightly; vibrate in place
LiquidTakes the shape of its containerDefiniteClose together; slide past one another
GasFills its containerFills its containerFar apart; move fast in all directions

A liquid poured from a tall glass into a wide bowl changes shape but keeps the same volume. A gas released into a room spreads out to fill the whole room.

check.prompt: A sample keeps the same volume when it is poured into a new container, but it takes the shape of that container. Its particles are close together and slide past one another. What state is the sample in?
options: Liquid
Solid
Gas
Plasma
why: A solid keeps its own shape; it does not take the shape of its container. Its particles vibrate in place instead of sliding past one another.
A gas does not keep the same volume; it spreads out to fill whatever container it is in. Its particles are far apart, not close together.
Plasma is an extremely hot, electrically charged state found in stars and lightning, not a sample you pour. The description of close, sliding particles matches a liquid.
check.hint: Which state has a definite volume but no definite shape?
check.explain: Keeping its volume but taking the container's shape, with particles close together that slide past one another, describes a liquid. A solid keeps both its shape and volume; a gas keeps neither.

screens.title: Phase changes and heating curves
screens.html:
Adding heat makes particles move faster. When they move fast enough, the substance changes state:

  • Melting: solid → liquid. Freezing is the reverse.
  • Evaporation or boiling: liquid → gas. Condensation is the reverse.
  • Sublimation: solid → gas directly (dry ice).

A heating curve shows temperature over time as heat is added at a steady rate. The rising parts show one state warming up. The flat parts show a phase change: the heat is used to pull particles apart, so the temperature does not rise until the change is complete. The lower flat part is melting; the higher flat part is boiling.

example.prompt: Use the heating curve of water. For how many minutes does the water boil, and at what temperature?
steps: Find the higher flat part of the line. It sits at 100 °C.
It starts at 14 minutes and ends at 20 minutes.
20 − 14 = 6 minutes.

check.prompt: Use the heating curve of water on this screen. For how many minutes does the ice melt?

mistakes.why: 6 minutes is when melting ends, not how long it lasts. Subtract the start time of the lower flat part (2 minutes) from its end time (6 minutes).
0 is the melting temperature in °C, read from the y-axis. The question asks for time, so read the length of the flat part along the x-axis.
2 minutes is when melting starts. The flat part runs from 2 to 6 minutes, so it lasts 6 − 2 minutes.

check.hint: Find the lower flat part of the line. When does it start and when does it end?
check.explain:
Melting is the lower flat part of the curve, at 0 °C. It starts at 2 minutes and ends at 6 minutes.

6 − 2 = 4 minutes.

Answering 6 reads only the end time; the length of the phase change is the end time minus the start time.

screens.title: Inside the atom
screens.html:
Every element is made of atoms. An atom has a tiny center called the nucleus, which holds protons (positive charge) and neutrons (no charge). Electrons (negative charge) move around the nucleus and have very little mass.

Atomic number = number of protons (this decides which element it is)
Mass number = protons + neutrons
Neutrons = mass number − atomic number
Neutral atom: electrons = protons

Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons are isotopes (carbon-12 and carbon-14). An atom that gains or loses electrons is a charged ion, but it is still the same element.

example.prompt: Chlorine has atomic number 17. A chlorine atom has mass number 35. Find its protons, neutrons, and electrons if it is neutral.
steps: Protons = atomic number = 17.
Neutrons = 35 − 17 = 18.
Neutral atom: electrons = protons = 17.

check.prompt: Aluminum has atomic number 13. An aluminum atom has mass number 27. How many neutrons does it have?

mistakes.why: 27 is the mass number, which counts protons and neutrons together. Subtract the 13 protons to get the neutrons.
You added the atomic number and the mass number. The mass number already includes the protons, so subtract: 27 − 13.
13 is the number of protons (the atomic number). Neutrons = mass number − atomic number.

check.explain:
Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 27 − 13 = 14.

Answering 27 uses the whole mass number, which also counts the 13 protons.

screens.title: The periodic table
screens.html:
The periodic table lists the elements in order of atomic number. Its layout predicts how elements behave:

  • Rows are called periods. Properties change as you move across a row.
  • Columns are called groups. Elements in the same group have the same number of outer electrons, so they have similar chemical properties.
  • Metals are on the left and in the middle; nonmetals are on the right.
GroupExamplesBehavior
1Lithium, sodium, potassiumSoft metals; react strongly with water
17Fluorine, chlorine, bromineVery reactive nonmetals
18Helium, neon, argonNoble gases; rarely react

To predict behavior, look up or down the column, not across the row.

check.prompt: Lithium (Group 1) reacts quickly with water and forms a basic solution. Which element would most likely react in a similar way?
options: Sodium, which is in Group 1
Beryllium, which is next to lithium in Period 2
Helium, which has an atomic number close to lithium's
Neon, which is in the same period as lithium
why: Beryllium sits next to lithium in the same row. Elements in a row do not share properties; elements in the same column (group) do.
Helium is a noble gas in Group 18 and almost never reacts. A close atomic number does not mean similar behavior; the group does.
Neon is in the same period (row) as lithium, but it is a noble gas that rarely reacts. Look down lithium's column instead.
check.hint: Elements in the same column of the periodic table behave alike.
check.explain:
Elements in the same group (column) have the same number of outer electrons, so they react in similar ways. Sodium is in Group 1 with lithium, so it also reacts quickly with water.

Beryllium and neon are in lithium's row, and properties change across a row. Helium is a noble gas that rarely reacts.

screens.title: Elements, compounds, and mixtures
screens.html:
• An element is made of only one kind of atom: iron (Fe), gold (Au), oxygen gas (O2).
  • A compound is two or more different elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio: water (H2O), carbon dioxide (CO2), table salt (NaCl). A compound can be very different from its elements: sodium is a reactive metal and chlorine is a poison gas, but NaCl is table salt.
  • A mixture is two or more substances combined but not bonded, in any ratio: salt water, air, trail mix. Mixtures can be separated by physical means such as filtering, evaporating, or using a magnet.

Careful: O2 has two atoms, but both are oxygen, so it is an element, not a compound.

options: Carbon dioxide, CO<sub>2</sub>
Oxygen gas, O<sub>2</sub>
Salt dissolved in water
Pure copper wire, Cu
why: O<sub>2</sub> has two atoms, but both are oxygen. Only one kind of atom means it is an element. A compound needs two or more different elements bonded together.
Salt water is a mixture: the salt and water are not bonded to each other, and you can separate them by evaporating the water.
Copper wire contains only copper atoms, so it is an element. A compound must contain at least two different elements.
check.hint: A compound has two or more different kinds of atoms bonded together in a fixed ratio.
check.explain:
Carbon dioxide contains two different elements, carbon and oxygen, bonded in a fixed 1 : 2 ratio, so it is a compound.

O2 and copper contain only one kind of atom each, so they are elements. Salt water is a mixture because the salt and water are not bonded and can be separated by evaporation.

screens.title: Physical and chemical changes
screens.html:
A physical change alters size, shape, or state, but the substance stays the same: melting ice, chopping wood, dissolving sugar, boiling water. Dissolved sugar is still sugar; you can get it back by evaporating the water.

A chemical change (a chemical reaction) makes one or more new substances: burning wood, rusting iron, baking bread, souring milk.

Evidence of a chemical change: a new gas (bubbles that are not from boiling), a color change, heat or light given off, a new solid (precipitate) forming when two liquids are mixed, or a new odor.

The test is always the same question: Is there a new substance? "It cannot be undone" is not the test; a shattered glass cannot be put back together, but it is still glass.

check.prompt: Sort each change into the correct category.
choices: A puddle dries up on a sunny day
A cake bakes in the oven
Butter melts in a hot pan
An antacid tablet fizzes in water
check.why: The most common mistake is putting the shattered bottle under chemical change because it cannot be repaired. The pieces are still glass, so it is a physical change. The fizzing tablet is chemical because the bubbles are a new gas.
check.hint: For each one, ask: is a new substance formed?
check.explain:
Physical: the puddle drying (water becomes water vapor), the bottle shattering (still glass), and butter melting (still butter).

Chemical: baking a cake (new substances, new texture and color), a match burning (heat, light, smoke, and ash), and the antacid fizzing (a new gas forms).

screens.title: Reading formulas and equations
screens.html:
A chemical formula shows the atoms in a substance. The small number written low after a symbol is a subscript: it tells how many of that atom. No subscript means one. H2O has 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom.

A chemical equation shows a reaction. The starting substances, the reactants, are on the left of the arrow. The new substances, the products, are on the right.

A big number in front of a formula is a coefficient. It multiplies every atom in that formula:

2H2O → H: 2 × 2 = 4 atoms; O: 2 × 1 = 2 atoms

3CO2 → C: 3 × 1 = 3 atoms; O: 3 × 2 = 6 atoms

mistakes.why: 1 is the oxygen in one water molecule. The coefficient 4 means four water molecules, so multiply: 4 × 1.
8 is the number of hydrogen atoms (4 × 2). The question asks about oxygen, which has no subscript, so each water has one.
You added the coefficient and the subscript (4 + 1). A coefficient multiplies: 4 × 1 = 4.

check.hint: The coefficient multiplies the number of oxygen atoms in one H<sub>2</sub>O.
check.explain:
One H2O has 1 oxygen atom (no subscript after O). The coefficient 4 means four molecules: 4 × 1 = 4 oxygen atoms.

8 is the number of hydrogen atoms (4 × 2), not oxygen.

screens.title: Balancing equations
screens.html:
An equation must be balanced: the same number of each kind of atom on both sides. Follow these steps:

  1. Count each kind of atom on each side. A small chart helps.
  2. Change only coefficients. Never change subscripts: H2O2 is hydrogen peroxide, not water.
  3. Balance elements that appear in only one substance on each side first. Save hydrogen, oxygen, or a lone element (like O2) for last.
  4. If one side has 2 of an atom and the other has 3, aim for 6 (the least common multiple).
  5. Recount everything, and use the smallest whole numbers.

steps: Count. Left: N 2, H 2. Right: N 1, H 3.
Nitrogen: write 2NH<sub>3</sub>. Now the right has N 2 and H 2 × 3 = 6.
Hydrogen: the left needs 6, so write 3H<sub>2</sub> (3 × 2 = 6).
Recount: N 2 = 2, H 6 = 6.

check.prompt:
Sodium metal reacts with chlorine gas to make table salt. Choose the coefficients that balance the equation using the smallest whole numbers. (A coefficient of 1 is shown here, although it is usually left unwritten.)

{{0}} Na + {{1}} Cl2 → {{2}} NaCl

why: With 1 Na on the left, the right side (2NaCl) has 2 Na, so sodium is unbalanced.
3 Na would not match the 2 Na in 2NaCl.
4 Na would require 4NaCl, which needs 2Cl<sub>2</sub>; that is not the smallest set of whole numbers.
2Cl<sub>2</sub> gives 4 Cl atoms, but 2NaCl has only 2 Cl. One Cl<sub>2</sub> already supplies 2.
3Cl<sub>2</sub> gives 6 Cl atoms, far more than the 2 in 2NaCl.
4Cl<sub>2</sub> gives 8 Cl atoms; the products have only 2.
1 NaCl has only 1 Cl atom, but Cl<sub>2</sub> brings 2. You need 2NaCl to use both chlorine atoms.
3NaCl would have 3 Cl atoms, an odd number that Cl<sub>2</sub> molecules (2 each) cannot match with these coefficients.
4NaCl has 4 Cl atoms and would need 2Cl<sub>2</sub> and 4Na; balanced, but not the smallest whole numbers.

check.hint: Cl<sub>2</sub> brings 2 chlorine atoms, but each NaCl holds only 1. Fix chlorine first, then sodium.
check.explain:
Count: left Na 1, Cl 2; right Na 1, Cl 1.

Chlorine: write 2NaCl so the right has 2 Cl. Now the right has 2 Na.

Sodium: write 2Na on the left.

Check: Na 2 = 2; Cl 2 = 2. 2Na + Cl2 → 2NaCl.

Writing 1, 1, 1 leaves chlorine at 2 on the left and 1 on the right.

screens.title: Conservation of mass
screens.html:
The law of conservation of mass says matter is not created or destroyed in a chemical reaction. The atoms are only rearranged into new substances. So:

Total mass of reactants = total mass of products

That is why equations must be balanced: the atoms that go in must all come out. You can use this rule to find a missing mass. If 12 g of carbon reacts completely with 32 g of oxygen, the carbon dioxide formed has a mass of 12 g + 32 g = 44 g. If you know the total and one part, subtract to find the other part.

check.prompt: In a sealed tube, 5.6 g of iron reacts completely with 3.2 g of sulfur to form iron sulfide. Nothing else is produced. What is the mass of the iron sulfide?

mistakes.why: You subtracted 3.2 from 5.6. In a reaction, the product contains all the atoms of both reactants, so add the masses.
That is the mass of the iron alone. The sulfur atoms are also part of the product, so add 3.2 g.

check.hint: Every atom of both reactants ends up in the product.
check.explain:
By conservation of mass, mass of products = mass of reactants.

5.6 g + 3.2 g = 8.8 g of iron sulfide.

Subtracting (2.4 g) would mean mass was lost, which a sealed reaction cannot do.

screens.title: Open and sealed containers
screens.html:
Sometimes a lab scale seems to break the law of conservation of mass. It never really does. Ask: was the container open, and is a gas involved?

  • Mass seems to drop: a gas product escaped from an open container before it was weighed. Baking soda and vinegar fizz out carbon dioxide; a burning candle sends carbon dioxide and water vapor into the air.
  • Mass seems to rise: a gas from the air joined the product. Steel wool burned in an open dish gains mass because oxygen from the air combines with the iron.
  • Sealed container: nothing gets in or out, so the total mass stays exactly the same.

check.prompt: A student weighs a candle, burns it on the scale in an open room for 30 minutes, and finds it is 4 g lighter. Which explanation is best?
options: The wax reacted with oxygen to form gases that drifted away without being weighed.
Burning destroyed 4 g of wax, turning that matter into heat and light energy.
The wax melted and changed state, and liquids have less mass than solids.
The flame made the candle lighter by pushing the scale upward with hot air.
why: Matter is not destroyed in a chemical reaction. The 4 g still exists; it left as carbon dioxide and water vapor.
Melting is a physical change and does not change mass. The mass loss comes from gases leaving the open room's scale.
The scale reading went down because matter left, not because of air pushing on it. Look for a gas product and an open container.
check.hint: Burning wax makes carbon dioxide and water vapor. Where do gases go in an open room?
check.explain:
Burning is a chemical change: the wax reacts with oxygen to make carbon dioxide and water vapor. In an open room these gases drift away, so the scale does not weigh them.

The mass was not destroyed. If the candle burned inside a sealed container on the scale, the total mass would stay the same.

screens.title: Density
screens.html:
Density is how much mass is packed into a certain volume.

Density = mass ÷ volume   (D = m ÷ V)

Units: g/mL or g/cm3. 1 mL = 1 cm3.

To find the volume of an odd-shaped object, use water displacement: read the water level in a graduated cylinder, add the object, and read the new level. The object's volume is the rise: final level − starting level.

Density is a property of the substance, not the size of the object. A small iron nail and a large iron bar have the same density, so density helps identify an unknown material.

example.prompt: A bolt has a mass of 78.7 g. The water level rises from 40.0 mL to 50.0 mL (see the picture). Find its density.
steps: Volume = 50.0 mL − 40.0 mL = 10.0 mL.
Density = 78.7 g ÷ 10.0 mL = 7.87 g/mL.
7.87 g/cm<sup>3</sup> matches iron.

check.prompt: A rock has a mass of 45 g. A graduated cylinder holds 25.0 mL of water. After the rock is added, the level is 40.0 mL. What is the rock's density?

mistakes.why: You divided by the final water level, 40.0 mL. The rock's volume is only the rise: 40.0 − 25.0 = 15.0 mL.
You divided by the starting water level, 25.0 mL. Use the change in level, 15.0 mL, as the rock's volume.
You divided volume by mass. Density is mass divided by volume: 45 ÷ 15.

check.hint: First find the rock's volume from the change in water level.
check.explain:
Volume = 40.0 mL − 25.0 mL = 15.0 mL.

Density = 45 g ÷ 15.0 mL = 3.0 g/mL.

Dividing by 40.0 mL (giving about 1.13) uses the final level instead of the rise.

screens.title: Float or sink?
screens.html:
Water has a density of 1.00 g/mL. Compare any object's density with water's:

  • Density less than 1.00 g/mL: the object floats (cork, most wood, ice at 0.92 g/mL).
  • Density greater than 1.00 g/mL: the object sinks (stone, most metals).

Heavy does not mean it sinks. A huge log floats because its mass is spread through a large volume; its density is under 1.00. A tiny pebble sinks because its density is over 1.00. Always calculate the density; do not judge by mass alone.

The same idea works for liquids: oil (about 0.9 g/mL) floats on water, and in a column of liquids the densest one settles to the bottom.

check.prompt: A plastic toy has a mass of 120 g and a volume of 150 cm3. What happens when it is placed in water?
options: It floats, because its density is 0.80 g/cm<sup>3</sup>, which is less than water's.
It sinks, because its density is 1.25 g/cm<sup>3</sup>, which is more than water's.
It sinks, because its mass of 120 g is more than 100 g, so it is too heavy.
It floats, because its density is 30 g/cm<sup>3</sup>, the difference of its volume and mass.
why: 1.25 comes from dividing volume by mass (150 ÷ 120). Density is mass ÷ volume: 120 ÷ 150 = 0.80.
Mass alone does not decide floating; density does. A heavy log can float if its mass is spread over a large volume.
Density is found by dividing mass by volume, not subtracting. 150 − 120 = 30 has no meaning as a density.
check.hint: Find the density with D = m ÷ V, then compare it with 1.00.
check.explain:
D = 120 g ÷ 150 cm3 = 0.80 g/cm3.

0.80 < 1.00, so the toy floats.

The tempting error is 150 ÷ 120 = 1.25, which flips the formula.

screens.title: Solutions and concentration
screens.html:
A solution is an even mixture of one substance dissolved in another. The solute is what dissolves (sugar, salt). The solvent does the dissolving (usually water).

Concentration tells how much solute is in a certain amount of solution:

Concentration (g/L) = grams of solute ÷ liters of solution

Convert mL to L first: divide by 1,000. 250 mL = 0.250 L.

Diluting: adding water does not change the amount of solute. It increases the volume, so the concentration goes down. To find a new concentration, first find the grams of solute, then divide by the new total volume.

example.prompt: A sports drink has 24 g of sugar in 400 mL. What is the sugar concentration in g/L?
steps: Concentration = 24 g ÷ 0.400 L = 60 g/L.

check.prompt: A cook dissolves 15 g of salt in water to make 250 mL of brine. What is the concentration of the brine in g/L?

mistakes.why: You divided by 250 without converting milliliters to liters. 250 mL = 0.250 L, and 15 ÷ 0.250 = 60.
You divided the volume by the mass. Concentration is grams of solute divided by liters of solution.
You multiplied 15 by 250. Concentration divides grams by liters: 15 ÷ 0.250.

check.hint: Change 250 mL to liters first, then divide grams by liters.
check.explain:
250 mL = 0.250 L.

Concentration = 15 g ÷ 0.250 L = 60 g/L.

Dividing by 250 without converting gives 0.06, which is grams per milliliter, not grams per liter.

screens.title: Solubility and temperature
screens.html:
Solubility is the greatest amount of solute that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent at a given temperature, often written as grams per 100 g of water. A solution at that limit is saturated; one below the limit is unsaturated.

  • Most solids dissolve more in warmer water (see the graph).
  • Gases dissolve less in warmer liquid, which is why warm soda goes flat.

Crystals on cooling: if you cool a solution, any solute above the new, lower limit comes out as solid crystals.

Crystals = amount actually dissolved − limit at the new temperature

Always start from the amount the student actually dissolved, not from the solubility limit at the high temperature.

example.prompt: A student dissolves 50 g of potassium chloride in 100 g of water at 80 °C (limit 51 g), then cools it to 20 °C (limit 34 g). How many grams come out as crystals?
steps: At 80 °C, 50 g < 51 g, so all 50 g dissolves.
At 20 °C, only 34 g can stay dissolved.

check.prompt: Use the graph. A student dissolves 60 g of potassium nitrate in 100 g of water at 40 °C. She then cools the solution to 20 °C. How many grams of potassium nitrate come out as crystals?

mistakes.why: You subtracted the two limits (64 − 32). The student dissolved only 60 g, not 64 g. Start from 60 g: 60 − 32.
You subtracted 60 from the 40 °C limit (64). That is how much more could have dissolved at 40 °C, not what comes out at 20 °C.

check.hint: Check that all 60 g dissolved at 40 °C. Then find how much can stay dissolved at 20 °C.
check.explain:
At 40 °C the limit for potassium nitrate is 64 g per 100 g water. 60 g < 64 g, so all 60 g dissolves.

At 20 °C the limit is 32 g.

Crystals = 60 g − 32 g = 28 g.

32 g (64 − 32) would be right only if the solution had been saturated with 64 g at 40 °C.

screens.title: Acids, bases, and the pH scale
screens.html:
The pH scale runs from 0 to 14 and measures how acidic or basic a solution is.

pHTypeEveryday examples
Below 7Acid (sour)Lemon juice 2, vinegar 3, tomato juice 4
7NeutralPure water
Above 7Base (bitter, slippery)Baking soda 9, ammonia 11

The lower the pH, the more acidic. The higher the pH, the more basic. A pH close to 7 is only weakly acidic or weakly basic; it is not neutral unless it is 7.

When an acid and a base are mixed, they neutralize each other and the pH moves toward 7. That is why an antacid (a base) eases stomach acid.

check.prompt: Use the graph on this screen. Which two substances are bases? Select two answers.
options: Ammonia
Baking soda
Milk
Pure water
Tomato juice
why: Milk has pH 6, which is below 7, so it is a weak acid. Being close to 7 does not make it a base.
Pure water has pH 7, which is neutral: neither an acid nor a base.
Tomato juice has pH 4, which is below 7, so it is an acid.
check.explain:
Bases have a pH above 7: baking soda (9) and ammonia (11).

Milk (6) and tomato juice (4) are acids because they are below 7. Pure water (7) is neutral.

screens.title: pH counts by powers of 10
screens.html:
The most tested pH fact on the GED: each 1-unit step on the pH scale is a factor of 10.

1 unit apart = 10 times
2 units apart = 10 × 10 = 100 times
3 units apart = 10 × 10 × 10 = 1,000 times

Method: subtract the two pH values to get the number of steps. Then multiply 10 by itself that many times. The solution with the lower pH is the more acidic one.

Two traps to avoid: the difference alone ("3 times") and the difference times 10 ("30 times"). Neither one uses the powers of 10.

example.prompt: Rainwater has pH 4. A lake has pH 7. How many times more acidic is the rain?
steps: Difference: 7 − 4 = 3 units.

check.prompt: Lemon juice has pH 2. Tomato juice has pH 4. How many times more acidic is lemon juice than tomato juice?

mistakes.why: 2 is the difference in pH units. Each unit is a factor of 10, so 2 units is 10 × 10.
You multiplied the difference by 10. The factors of 10 multiply together: 10 × 10 = 100.
10 times is a 1-unit difference. These pH values are 2 units apart, so it is 10 × 10.

check.hint: Find the difference in pH, then use one factor of 10 for each unit.
check.explain:
Difference: 4 − 2 = 2 units.

10 × 10 = 100 times more acidic.

Answering 20 multiplies the difference by 10 instead of multiplying the 10s together.

screens.title: Summary
screens.html:
• States: solid (fixed shape and volume), liquid (fixed volume), gas (neither). Flat parts of a heating curve = phase changes.
  • Atoms: protons = atomic number; neutrons = mass number − atomic number; neutral atom: electrons = protons. Same group = similar properties.
  • Matter: element (one kind of atom), compound (bonded, fixed ratio), mixture (not bonded).
  • Changes: chemical = new substance (gas, color, heat or light, precipitate). Physical = same substance.
  • Equations: change coefficients only. Mass of reactants = mass of products. Open container + gas = mass seems to change.
  • Density = m ÷ V; water = 1.00 g/mL. Concentration = g ÷ L. Crystals = dissolved − new limit.
  • pH: below 7 acid, 7 neutral, above 7 base; each unit = 10 times.

Next, go to Practice and start with Set A.

items.prompt: A substance has no definite shape and no definite volume. Its particles are far apart and move quickly in all directions. In which state of matter is this substance?
options: Gas
Liquid
Solid
Crystal
why: A liquid has a definite volume; it only takes the shape of its container. The sample described has no definite volume, so it is not a liquid.
A solid has both a definite shape and a definite volume, and its particles vibrate in place instead of moving freely in all directions.
A crystal is a kind of solid with particles locked in a regular pattern. Fast, far-apart particles describe a gas.
items.hint: Which state spreads out to fill any container it is in?
items.explain:
A gas has no definite shape or volume; it spreads out to fill its container because its particles are far apart and moving fast.

A liquid has a definite volume (it only takes the shape of its container), so it does not fit. A solid has both a definite shape and a definite volume. A crystal is a type of solid, with particles locked in a regular pattern.

items.prompt: Sodium has an atomic number of 11. A neutral sodium atom has a mass number of 23. Which choice correctly describes this atom?
options: 11 protons, 12 neutrons, 11 electrons
11 protons, 11 neutrons, 12 electrons
12 protons, 11 neutrons, 12 electrons
23 protons, 11 neutrons, 23 electrons
why: You swapped the neutrons and electrons. In a neutral atom, electrons equal protons (11); neutrons are 23 − 11 = 12.
You used the neutron count as the proton count. Protons always equal the atomic number, 11.
You used the mass number (23) as the number of protons. The atomic number, 11, gives the protons.
items.hint: Atomic number tells you the protons. Subtract it from the mass number to get the neutrons.
items.explain:
Protons = atomic number = 11.

Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 23 − 11 = 12.

In a neutral atom, electrons = protons = 11.

The choice with 23 protons uses the mass number as the proton count, which is a common error. The choice with 12 electrons would describe a charged ion, not a neutral atom.

items.prompt: Sort each change into the correct category.
choices: Ice cream melting on a hot day
items.why: The most common mistake is putting sugar dissolving under chemical change because the sugar seems to disappear. It is still sugar and could be recovered by evaporating the tea, so it is physical. Souring milk is chemical because bacteria make a new acid.
items.hint: Ask: is a new substance formed, or is it still the same substance in a different form?
items.explain:
Physical changes (same substance, new form or state): melting ice cream, tearing paper, and dissolving sugar. The dissolved sugar is still sugar and could be recovered by evaporating the water.

Chemical changes (new substances form): rusting (iron combines with oxygen to form iron oxide), burning wood (forms ash, carbon dioxide, and water vapor and gives off heat and light), and souring milk (bacteria produce acid, which changes the taste and texture).

items.prompt: Based on the data, the solubility of which salt is least affected by a change in temperature?
options: Sodium chloride
Potassium chloride
Potassium nitrate
All three salts are affected equally.
why: Potassium chloride changes from 28 g to 51 g, a change of 23 g. Sodium chloride changes only 2 g, so it is less affected.
Potassium nitrate changes the most (from 13 g to 169 g). The question asks which is affected the least.
The changes are very different: 2 g, 23 g, and 156 g. Compare each salt's value at 0 °C with its value at 80 °C.
items.hint: For each salt, compare its value at 0 °C with its value at 80 °C.
items.explain:
Change in solubility from 0 °C to 80 °C:

  • Sodium chloride: 38 − 36 = 2 g
  • Potassium chloride: 51 − 28 = 23 g
  • Potassium nitrate: 169 − 13 = 156 g

Sodium chloride changes the least; its line on the graph is nearly flat. Potassium nitrate is the most affected, which is the opposite of what the question asks.

items.prompt: Based on the data, what is the melting point of Substance X?

mistakes.why: 20 °C is the starting temperature, when the substance was still a solid warming up. The melting point is the flat part, where solid and liquid are both present.
140 °C is the last reading, after the substance was already liquid. Look for the temperature that stays constant while the solid turns to liquid.
6 is the time in minutes when melting began, read from the x-axis. The question asks for a temperature, so read the y-axis value of the flat part.

items.hint: During melting, the temperature stops rising. Find the flat part of the curve.
items.explain:
From 6 to 12 minutes, the temperature stays at 80 °C even though heat is still being added. This is the same time the student saw the solid turning to liquid. The heat is being used to pull particles apart, not to raise the temperature, so the flat part shows the melting point: 80 °C.

20 °C is only the starting temperature, and 6 is a time, not a temperature.

why: Argon sits next to chlorine in the same row, but it is a noble gas (Group 18) that rarely reacts. Similar properties come from being in the same column.
Sodium is in the same row (Period 3) as chlorine, but it is a Group 1 metal. Elements in a row do not share chemical properties.

items.hint: Elements in the same column (group) have similar chemical properties.
items.explain:
Elements in the same group have the same number of outer electrons, so they react in similar ways. Chlorine is in Group 17, and bromine is directly below it in the same group. (Bromine is, in fact, used to disinfect hot tubs.)

Argon, sodium, and magnesium share chlorine's row, not its column. Argon is especially tempting because it is right next to chlorine, but it is a noble gas that almost never reacts.

items.prompt: What is the density of Sample A? Round to the nearest hundredth.

mistakes.why: You divided by the final water level, 70.0 mL. The sample's volume is only the rise in the water level: 70.0 − 50.0 = 20.0 mL.
You divided by the starting water level, 50.0 mL. Use the change in level, 20.0 mL, as the sample's volume.
You divided volume by mass (20.0 ÷ 54.0). Density is mass divided by volume.

items.hint: The sample's volume is the change in the water level. Then divide mass by volume.
items.explain:
Volume of Sample A = 70.0 mL − 50.0 mL = 20.0 mL.

Density = mass ÷ volume = 54.0 g ÷ 20.0 mL = 2.70 g/mL.

A common error is dividing by the final water level: 54.0 ÷ 70.0 ≈ 0.77 g/mL. The volume of the sample is only the rise in the water level. The correct value, 2.70 g/mL, matches aluminum in the reference table.
