items.prompt:
Hydrogen gas burns in oxygen to form water. Choose the coefficients that balance the equation using the smallest whole numbers. (A coefficient of 1 is shown here, although it is usually left unwritten.)

{{0}} H2 + {{1}} O2 → {{2}} H2O

why: One H<sub>2</sub> gives only 2 H atoms, but 2H<sub>2</sub>O has 4 H atoms.
3H<sub>2</sub> gives 6 H atoms, but 2H<sub>2</sub>O has only 4.
4H<sub>2</sub> gives 8 H atoms. That would need 4H<sub>2</sub>O and 2O<sub>2</sub>: balanced, but not the smallest whole numbers.
2O<sub>2</sub> gives 4 O atoms, but 2H<sub>2</sub>O has only 2 O atoms.
3O<sub>2</sub> gives 6 O atoms, but 2H<sub>2</sub>O has only 2.
4O<sub>2</sub> gives 8 O atoms, far more than the 2 in 2H<sub>2</sub>O.
One H<sub>2</sub>O has only 1 O atom, but O<sub>2</sub> brings 2. You need 2H<sub>2</sub>O to use both.
3H<sub>2</sub>O has 3 O atoms, an odd number; O<sub>2</sub> molecules supply oxygen in pairs, so this cannot balance with these choices.
4H<sub>2</sub>O balances only with 4H<sub>2</sub> and 2O<sub>2</sub>, which is not the smallest set of whole numbers.

items.hint: Balance oxygen first: O<sub>2</sub> has 2 oxygen atoms, but each H<sub>2</sub>O has only 1.
items.explain:
Unbalanced count: left H 2, O 2; right H 2, O 1.

Oxygen: put 2 in front of H2O, giving O 2 on the right. Now hydrogen on the right is 2 × 2 = 4.

Hydrogen: put 2 in front of H2, giving 2 × 2 = 4 on the left.

Check: H 4 = 4; O 2 = 2. 2H2 + 1O2 → 2H2O, written as 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O.

Choosing 1, 1, 1 leaves oxygen unbalanced (2 on the left, 1 on the right). You cannot fix it by changing H2O to H2O2, because that would make a different substance.

items.prompt: Which statement best explains why the total mass decreased in Trial 1 but not in Trial 2?
options: In Trial 1, carbon dioxide gas escaped into the air and was not weighed; in Trial 2, the gas was trapped inside the bottle.
In Trial 1, about 1.10 g of matter was destroyed by the reaction; in Trial 2, the cap prevented the reaction from destroying matter.
In Trial 1, the reaction did not follow the law of conservation of mass because the flask was made of glass.
In Trial 2, the baking soda and vinegar did not react, so no mass was lost.
why: Matter is never destroyed in a chemical reaction. The 1.10 g still exists as carbon dioxide gas that left the open flask.
The law of conservation of mass holds no matter what the container is made of. What mattered was that the flask was open, so the gas escaped.
The fizzing described in Trial 2 shows the reaction did happen. The mass stayed the same because the sealed bottle kept the gas inside.
items.hint: Look at the products in the equation. Which one is a gas? Where could it go in an open flask?
items.explain:
One product of the reaction is carbon dioxide (CO2), a gas. In the open flask of Trial 1, the gas bubbled out into the room, so the balance did not weigh it. The mass of the escaped gas is 182.40 g − 181.30 g = 1.10 g.

In the sealed bottle of Trial 2, all products, including the gas, stayed inside, so the total mass stayed at 183.10 g. This supports the law of conservation of mass.

Matter is never destroyed in a chemical reaction, so the choice that says 1.10 g was destroyed is wrong. The fizzing described in Trial 2 shows that a reaction did happen there.

items.prompt: A student dissolves 100 g of potassium nitrate in 100 g of water at 60 °C. She then cools the solution to 20 °C. About how many grams of potassium nitrate will come out of the solution as solid crystals?
why: 32 g is the amount that can stay dissolved at 20 °C. The question asks how much comes out: 100 − 32.
You subtracted the two solubilities (110 − 32). The student dissolved only 100 g, not 110 g, so start from 100 g.
Cooling does not force all the solute out. At 20 °C, 32 g can still stay dissolved, so only 100 − 32 comes out.
items.hint: First check whether all 100 g dissolved at 60 °C. Then find how much can stay dissolved at 20 °C.
items.explain:
At 60 °C, up to 110 g can dissolve in 100 g of water. Since 100 g < 110 g, all 100 g dissolves.

At 20 °C, only 32 g can stay dissolved.

Crystals formed = 100 g − 32 g = 68 g.

78 g comes from subtracting the two solubilities (110 − 32), but the student dissolved only 100 g, not 110 g. 32 g is the amount that stays dissolved, not the amount that comes out.

items.prompt: Based on the table, which two statements are correct? Select two answers.
options: Lemon juice is 10 times more acidic than vinegar.
Ammonia cleaner is a base.
Black coffee is a base because its pH is closer to 7 than vinegar's pH is.
Distilled water is the most acidic substance in the table.
Baking soda solution is an acid because its pH is a single-digit number.
why: Black coffee has pH 5, which is below 7, so it is a weak acid. Being closer to 7 makes it a weaker acid, not a base.
Distilled water (pH 7) is neutral. The most acidic substance has the lowest pH: lemon juice (pH 2).
Baking soda solution has pH 9, which is above 7, so it is a base. The number of digits has nothing to do with it.
items.hint: pH below 7 is acidic and above 7 is basic. Each 1-unit difference in pH is a factor of 10.
items.explain:
Correct: Lemon juice (pH 2) and vinegar (pH 3) differ by 1 unit, and each unit is a factor of 10, so lemon juice is 10 times more acidic. Ammonia cleaner has a pH of 11, which is above 7, so it is a base.

Incorrect: Black coffee (pH 5) is below 7, so it is a weak acid, not a base. Being closer to 7 makes it a weaker acid, not a base. Distilled water (pH 7) is neutral; lemon juice, with the lowest pH, is the most acidic. Baking soda solution (pH 9) is above 7, so it is a base; whether the number has one digit or two does not matter.

items.prompt: A lab technician has 200 mL of a salt solution with a concentration of 30 g/L. She adds 100 mL of pure water and stirs. What is the concentration of the new solution?
options: 15 g/L
20 g/L
30 g/L
45 g/L
why: 15 g/L is what you get if the volume doubled (200 mL to 400 mL). Only 100 mL was added, so the new volume is 300 mL.
Adding water spreads the same 6 g of salt through more liquid, so the concentration must go down from 30 g/L.
45 g/L multiplies instead of divides (30 × 1.5). Adding water can only lower the concentration.
items.hint: Find how many grams of salt are in the original 200 mL. Adding water does not change the amount of salt, only the volume.
items.explain:
Salt in the original solution: 200 mL = 0.200 L, and 0.200 L × 30 g/L = 6 g of salt.

New volume: 200 mL + 100 mL = 300 mL = 0.300 L.

New concentration = 6 g ÷ 0.300 L = 20 g/L.

30 g/L assumes adding water does not change the concentration, but the same salt is now spread through more liquid. 15 g/L would be the result of doubling the volume (adding 200 mL), not adding 100 mL. 45 g/L multiplies instead of dividing; adding water can only lower the concentration.

items.prompt:
A student places 2.40 g of magnesium ribbon in an open crucible and heats it. The ribbon burns with a bright white light and turns into a white powder, magnesium oxide:

2Mg + O2 → 2MgO

All of the magnesium reacts, and the magnesium oxide has a mass of 4.00 g. How many grams of oxygen from the air combined with the magnesium?

mistakes.why: You added 2.40 and 4.00. The 4.00 g of product already includes the magnesium. Oxygen = product − magnesium.
Mass is conserved, but the crucible was open: oxygen from the air joined the magnesium. The product weighs more because it contains that oxygen.
2.40 g is the mass of the magnesium. The question asks for the oxygen, which is the extra mass in the product: 4.00 − 2.40.

items.hint: Mass of reactants = mass of products. The reactants are magnesium and oxygen; the product is magnesium oxide.
items.explain:
By conservation of mass: mass of magnesium + mass of oxygen = mass of magnesium oxide.

2.40 g + oxygen = 4.00 g, so oxygen = 4.00 − 2.40 = 1.60 g.

The product is heavier than the ribbon because oxygen from the air, which was never on the balance at the start, became part of it. Adding the two masses (6.40 g) double-counts the magnesium.

items.prompt: A student heats 10.0 g of a red-orange powder in a test tube. A colorless gas is given off, and shiny droplets of a liquid metal collect on the cooler part of the tube. The red-orange powder disappears completely. Tests show that the gas is oxygen and the metal is mercury, and neither can be broken down into simpler substances. Which conclusion about the red-orange powder is best supported?
options: It is a compound, because heating broke it down into two different elements.
It is an element, because the mercury produced cannot be broken down any further.
It is a mixture of mercury and oxygen that heating separated by physical means.
It went through a physical change, because heat changed it from a solid to a gas.
why: The mercury is a product, not the powder. The powder broke down into two substances, so it cannot be an element; an element has only one kind of atom.

A mixture of a liquid metal and a gas would not look like a red-orange powder; the powder had its own properties. Breaking it into new substances took a chemical change, which is the mark of a compound.
New substances with different properties (a gas and a liquid metal) formed, so this was a chemical change. A physical change would leave the same substance in a new form.
items.hint: The powder broke down into two different substances that are each elements. What kind of matter can be broken into elements by a chemical change?
items.explain:
The powder was broken down by heating into two different elements, oxygen and mercury. Each product looks and acts completely differently from the red-orange powder, which shows the elements had been chemically bonded. A substance made of two or more elements chemically bonded is a compound (this one is mercury oxide).

The tempting wrong answer calls the powder an element because the mercury cannot be broken down, but that describes a product, not the starting powder.

items.prompt: A pot of soup is heated on a stove from 20 °C to 60 °C. It does not boil. What happens to the water particles in the soup as it warms?
options: They move faster and spread slightly farther apart.
They move more slowly and pack together more tightly.
They stop moving until the soup reaches its boiling point.
They each grow larger as they absorb heat from the stove.
why: Slower, tighter particles describe cooling, not heating. Adding heat gives particles more energy, so they speed up.
Particles are always moving, at every temperature. Heating makes them move faster well before boiling.
The particles themselves do not grow. Heating makes them move faster and spread out a little, which is why the soup expands slightly.
items.hint: Think about what adding heat energy does to the motion of particles.
items.explain:
Adding heat gives the particles more energy, so they move faster and spread slightly farther apart. That is why most liquids expand a little when warmed.

Particles never stop moving, and they do not get bigger; only their speed and spacing change.

items.prompt: Zinc has an atomic number of 30. A neutral zinc atom has a mass number of 65. Which choice correctly describes this atom?
options: 30 protons, 35 neutrons, 30 electrons
30 protons, 30 neutrons, 35 electrons
35 protons, 30 neutrons, 35 electrons
65 protons, 30 neutrons, 65 electrons
why: You swapped the neutrons and electrons. In a neutral atom, electrons equal protons (30); neutrons are 65 − 30 = 35.
You used the neutron count as the proton count. Protons always equal the atomic number, 30.
You used the mass number (65) as the number of protons. The atomic number, 30, gives the protons.
items.hint: Atomic number = protons. Neutrons = mass number − atomic number. A neutral atom has as many electrons as protons.
items.explain:
Protons = atomic number = 30.

Neutrons = 65 − 30 = 35.

Neutral atom, so electrons = protons = 30.

The choice with 65 protons uses the mass number as the proton count, the most common error.

items.prompt: Sort each change into the correct category.
choices: Water vapor condensing on a cold window
Gasoline burning in a car engine
Salt dissolving in a pot of soup
Vinegar and baking soda bubbling when mixed
items.why: The most common mistake is putting the bubbling vinegar and baking soda under physical change because the bubbles look like boiling. The bubbles are a new gas, carbon dioxide, so it is a chemical change. Condensing water is still water, so it is physical.
items.hint: Ask: is a new substance formed, or is it the same substance in a new form?
items.explain:
Physical changes (same substance): water vapor condensing (still water), chopping wood (still wood), and salt dissolving (still salt; it can be recovered by evaporation).

Chemical changes (new substances): tarnish is a new black compound on the silver; burning gasoline makes carbon dioxide and water and releases heat; vinegar and baking soda make a new gas, carbon dioxide.

items.prompt: Based on the data, the solubility of which salt decreases as the temperature increases?
options: Lithium carbonate
Potassium bromide
Sodium nitrate
Each salt's solubility increases as the temperature increases.
why: Potassium bromide rises from 54 g to 95 g as the water warms, so its solubility increases.
Sodium nitrate rises from 73 g to 148 g; it shows the biggest increase, the opposite of what the question asks.
Lithium carbonate falls from 1.5 g at 0 °C to 0.9 g at 80 °C. Its small numbers make it easy to overlook on the graph, so check the table.
items.hint: For each salt, compare its value at 0 °C with its value at 80 °C. Which one goes down?
items.explain:
From 0 °C to 80 °C:

  • Sodium nitrate: 73 → 148 g (increases)
  • Potassium bromide: 54 → 95 g (increases)
  • Lithium carbonate: 1.5 → 0.9 g (decreases)

Lithium carbonate becomes less soluble as the water warms. Its values are so small that its line looks flat on the graph, which is why reading the table matters.

items.prompt: Based on the data, at what temperature does stearic acid freeze?

mistakes.why: 90 °C is the starting temperature, when the sample was a hot liquid. Freezing happens at the flat part of the curve, where liquid and solid are both present.
42 °C is the last reading, after the sample was already solid and cooling further. Look for the temperature that stays constant while the liquid turns solid.
6 is the time in minutes when freezing began, read from the x-axis. The question asks for a temperature, so read the y-axis value of the flat part.

items.hint: While a liquid freezes, its temperature stops falling. Find the flat part of the curve.
items.explain:
From 6 to 12 minutes, the temperature stays at 69 °C even though the tube keeps losing heat. This is the same time the student saw solid wax forming. As particles lock together into a solid, they release energy, which keeps the temperature steady until freezing is complete. The freezing point is 69 °C (the same as its melting point).

90 °C is only the starting temperature, and 6 is a time, not a temperature.

items.prompt:
The table shows part of the periodic table.

Group 1Group 2Group 17Group 18
Lithium (Li), 3Beryllium (Be), 4Fluorine (F), 9Neon (Ne), 10
Sodium (Na), 11Magnesium (Mg), 12Chlorine (Cl), 17Argon (Ar), 18

The number after each name is the atomic number. Neon is used in glowing signs partly because it does not react with the metal parts inside the tube. Which element would most likely also be unreactive?
options: Argon
Sodium
Fluorine
Magnesium
why: Sodium has the next atomic number after neon (11), but it starts a new row in Group 1 and reacts violently with water. A close atomic number does not mean similar properties.
Fluorine is right next to neon in the same row, but it is a Group 17 element and one of the most reactive elements of all. Look down neon's column instead.
Magnesium is a Group 2 metal that reacts with oxygen and acids. It does not share neon's column, so it does not share neon's properties.
items.hint: Elements in the same column (group) have similar chemical properties.
items.explain:
Neon is in Group 18, the noble gases, which rarely react. Argon is directly below neon in the same group, so it is also unreactive. (Argon is used inside light bulbs for exactly this reason.)

Fluorine is tempting because it sits right beside neon, but elements in the same row do not share properties; fluorine is extremely reactive.

items.prompt: What is the density of Piece G? Round to the nearest tenth.

mistakes.why: You divided by the final water level, 45.0 mL. The piece's volume is only the rise in the water level: 45.0 − 40.0 = 5.0 mL.
You divided by the starting water level, 40.0 mL. Use the change in level, 5.0 mL, as the piece's volume.
You divided volume by mass (5.0 ÷ 52.5). Density is mass divided by volume.

items.hint: The piece's volume is the change in the water level. Then divide mass by volume.
items.explain:
Volume of Piece G = 45.0 mL − 40.0 mL = 5.0 mL.

Density = 52.5 g ÷ 5.0 mL = 10.5 g/mL, which matches silver.

Dividing by the final level (52.5 ÷ 45.0 ≈ 1.2) is the most common error; the piece takes up only the 5.0 mL the water rose.

items.prompt: Based on its density, Piece H is most likely made of which metal?
options: Nickel
Tin
Silver
Titanium
why: Tin's density, 7.31 g/cm<sup>3</sup>, matches Piece F (73.1 ÷ 10.0). Make sure you used Piece H's row: 89.1 ÷ 10.0 = 8.91.
Silver (10.5) matches Piece G. Picking the densest metal because Piece H has the largest mass skips the volume; density depends on both.
Titanium (4.51) matches Piece E. Piece H's density, 89.1 ÷ 10.0 = 8.91 g/cm<sup>3</sup>, is about twice as large.
items.hint: Find Piece H's volume from the water levels, calculate its density, and match it to the reference table.
items.explain:
Volume of Piece H = 35.0 mL − 25.0 mL = 10.0 mL = 10.0 cm3.

Density = 89.1 g ÷ 10.0 cm3 = 8.91 g/cm3, which matches nickel.

Choosing silver because Piece H is the heaviest piece is a common trap: Piece G is lighter but far denser, because its volume is only 5.0 mL.

items.prompt:
When aluminum metal is exposed to oxygen, it forms a thin coating of aluminum oxide. Choose the coefficients that balance the equation using the smallest whole numbers.

{{0}} Al + {{1}} O2 → {{2}} Al2O3

why: One Al does not match the 4 Al atoms in 2Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> (2 × 2 = 4).
2Al balances only a single Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>. With 2Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>, the right side has 4 Al.
3Al does not match the 4 Al atoms on the right.
One O<sub>2</sub> gives 2 O atoms, but 2Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> has 6.
2O<sub>2</sub> gives 4 O atoms, but 2Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> has 6.
4O<sub>2</sub> gives 8 O atoms, but 2Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> has only 6.
One Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> has 3 O atoms, an odd number. O<sub>2</sub> supplies oxygen in pairs, so you need an even count: 2Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> has 6.
3Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> has 9 O atoms, an odd number that O<sub>2</sub> pairs cannot match.
4Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> balances only with 8Al and 6O<sub>2</sub>, which is not the smallest set of whole numbers.

items.hint: Oxygen comes in 2s on the left and 3s on the right. What is the smallest number that both 2 and 3 divide into evenly?
items.explain:
Unbalanced count: left Al 1, O 2; right Al 2, O 3.

Oxygen: the least common multiple of 2 and 3 is 6. Use 3O2 (3 × 2 = 6) and 2Al2O3 (2 × 3 = 6).

Aluminum: the right side now has 2 × 2 = 4 Al, so use 4Al on the left.

Check: Al 4 = 4; O 6 = 6. 4Al + 3O2 → 2Al2O3.

A common wrong answer is 2Al + O2 → Al2O3; it balances aluminum (2 = 2) but leaves oxygen at 2 on the left and 3 on the right.

items.prompt: Which statement best explains why the total mass increased in Trial 1 but not in Trial 2?
options: In Trial 1, oxygen from the room joined the iron and had not been weighed at the start; in Trial 2, all the oxygen was sealed in from the start.
In Trial 1, the reaction created 1.20 g of new matter; in Trial 2, the sealed flask kept the reaction from creating any new matter.
In Trial 1, the dark solid is a new substance, and new substances always have more mass than the substances that formed them.
In Trial 2, the steel wool did not react at all, because the oxygen inside the sealed flask could not reach the iron strands.
why: Matter is never created in a chemical reaction. The extra 1.20 g was oxygen from the air that became part of the iron oxide.
New substances do not automatically weigh more. The product weighed more here only because oxygen from the room, which was not weighed at the start, joined the iron.
The strands glowed and turned dark and brittle in Trial 2 as well, so the reaction did happen. The mass stayed the same because nothing could enter or leave the flask.
items.hint: Look at the equation. Which reactant comes from the air? Could more of it reach the iron in an open dish?
items.explain:
The equation shows iron reacting with oxygen, O2. In the open dish, oxygen from the room kept reaching the iron and became part of the iron oxide. That oxygen was not on the balance at the start, so the mass rose by 61.20 − 60.00 = 1.20 g.

In the sealed flask, the oxygen that reacted was already inside when the flask was weighed, and nothing could get in or out, so the total stayed at 215.50 g. Both trials support the law of conservation of mass; no matter was created.

items.prompt: A student dissolves 120 g of sodium nitrate in 100 g of water at 60 °C. She then cools the solution to 20 °C. About how many grams of sodium nitrate will come out of the solution as solid crystals?
why: You subtracted the two solubilities (124 − 88). The student dissolved only 120 g, not 124 g, so start from 120 g.
88 g is the amount that can stay dissolved at 20 °C. The question asks how much comes out: 120 − 88.
Cooling does not force all the solute out. At 20 °C, 88 g can still stay dissolved, so only 120 − 88 comes out.
items.hint: First check whether all 120 g dissolved at 60 °C. Then find how much can stay dissolved at 20 °C.
items.explain:
At 60 °C, up to 124 g of sodium nitrate can dissolve in 100 g of water. Since 120 g < 124 g, all 120 g dissolves.

At 20 °C, only 88 g can stay dissolved.

Crystals formed = 120 g − 88 g = 32 g.

36 g comes from subtracting the two solubilities (124 − 88), but the student dissolved 120 g, not 124 g.

items.prompt: Based on the table, which two statements are correct? Select two answers.
options: Stomach acid is 100 times more acidic than orange juice.
Seawater is a weak base.
Milk is neutral because its pH is close to 7.
Soapy water is 2 times more basic than seawater.
Drain cleaner is the most acidic liquid because it has the highest pH.
why: Milk has pH 6, which is below 7, so it is a weak acid. Only a pH of exactly 7 is neutral.
Soapy water (10) and seawater (8) differ by 2 units, and each unit is a factor of 10: 10 × 10 = 100 times, not 2 times.
A high pH means basic, not acidic. Drain cleaner (pH 13) is the strongest base in the table; stomach acid (pH 1) is the most acidic.
items.hint: pH below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral, and above 7 is basic. Each 1-unit difference is a factor of 10.
items.explain:
Correct: Stomach acid (pH 1) and orange juice (pH 3) differ by 2 units, so stomach acid is 10 × 10 = 100 times more acidic. Seawater (pH 8) is just above 7, so it is a weak base.

Incorrect: Milk (pH 6) is a weak acid, not neutral. Soapy water is 100 times, not 2 times, more basic than seawater. Drain cleaner has the highest pH, which makes it the strongest base, not the strongest acid.

items.prompt: A pharmacy technician has 50 mL of a medicine solution with a concentration of 40 g/L. She adds water until the total volume is 250 mL and stirs. What is the concentration of the new solution?
options: 8 g/L
10 g/L
40 g/L
why: You divided the 2 g of medicine by 200 mL, the water added. The medicine is spread through the whole 250 mL, so divide by 0.250 L.
Adding water spreads the same 2 g of medicine through more liquid, so the concentration must go down from 40 g/L.
200 g/L multiplies by 5 instead of dividing. Making the volume 5 times larger makes the concentration 5 times smaller.
items.hint: Find how many grams of medicine are in the original 50 mL. Adding water does not change that amount, only the volume.
items.explain:
Medicine in the original solution: 50 mL = 0.050 L, and 0.050 L × 40 g/L = 2 g.

New volume: 250 mL = 0.250 L (the question gives the total).

New concentration = 2 g ÷ 0.250 L = 8 g/L.

10 g/L uses only the 200 mL of water that was added instead of the 250 mL total. Diluting can only lower the concentration, so 40 g/L and 200 g/L are impossible.

items.prompt:
Limestone is mostly calcium carbonate. When it is heated strongly in an open kiln, it breaks down into solid calcium oxide (lime) and carbon dioxide gas:

CaCO3 → CaO + CO2

A student heats 10.0 g of pure calcium carbonate in an open crucible until it has all reacted. The solid left behind has a mass of 5.6 g. How many grams of carbon dioxide were released?

mistakes.why: You added 10.0 and 5.6. The 10.0 g of calcium carbonate is the total that splits into two products. Carbon dioxide = 10.0 − 5.6.
5.6 g is the solid calcium oxide left behind. The carbon dioxide is the rest of the original 10.0 g.
Mass is conserved, but the crucible was open, so the carbon dioxide gas escaped. The missing mass on the balance is that gas.

items.hint: Mass of reactant = total mass of products. One product stayed in the crucible; the other escaped as a gas.
items.explain:
By conservation of mass: mass of CaCO3 = mass of CaO + mass of CO2.

10.0 g = 5.6 g + CO2, so CO2 = 10.0 − 5.6 = 4.4 g.

The solid loses mass on the balance because the carbon dioxide leaves the open crucible as a gas. Adding the masses (15.6 g) double-counts, because the calcium oxide came out of the original 10.0 g.

items.prompt: A student stirs a spoonful of gray powder into warm water. Part of the powder dissolves, and the rest sinks. She pours everything through filter paper. Black grains stay on the paper, and a magnet picks them up. She lets the clear liquid that passed through evaporate, and white crystals that taste salty are left in the dish. Which conclusion about the gray powder is best supported?
options: It was a mixture, because it was separated into different substances by physical means.
It was a compound, because it was made of more than one substance with different properties.
It was an element, because the black grains it contained were attracted to the magnet.
It went through a chemical change, because new white crystals formed when the liquid evaporated.
why: Containing more than one substance is not enough to make a compound. A compound's elements are bonded and can be separated only by a chemical change; here, filtering and evaporating separated the parts.
The black grains (likely iron) are only one part of the powder. A powder that splits into black grains and white salt contains more than one substance, so it cannot be an element.
The salt dissolved and then came back as the same salty crystals when the water evaporated. Dissolving and evaporating are physical changes.
items.hint: Which steps did the student use to separate the powder: physical steps or chemical reactions?
items.explain:
Stirring, filtering, using a magnet, and evaporating are all physical methods. They separated the gray powder into black magnetic grains and white salt without making any new substance. Substances that are combined but not bonded, and can be separated by physical means, form a mixture.

The tempting wrong answer calls it a compound because it contained more than one substance, but a compound's parts are chemically bonded and cannot be pulled apart by filtering or evaporating.

items.prompt: A pot of water on a stove reaches 100 °C and begins to boil. The burner stays on, but a thermometer in the water keeps reading 100 °C until the water is almost gone. Which statement best explains this?
options: The heat is pulling water particles apart into a gas instead of making them move faster.
The burner automatically stops supplying heat once the water reaches its boiling point.
The water particles stop moving while they change from the liquid state to the gas state.
The thermometer cannot measure any temperature higher than the boiling point of water.
why: The burner is still on and still adding heat; the problem says so. The heat is being used for the phase change instead of raising the temperature.
Particles never stop moving. During boiling they move fast enough to escape the liquid; the added energy separates them rather than speeding them up.
The thermometer is not the limit; steam above 100 °C can be measured. The flat reading happens because the energy goes into changing state.
items.explain:
During a phase change, the added heat is used to separate particles (liquid to gas), not to make them move faster, so the temperature stays flat at 100 °C until all the water has boiled. This is the flat part of a heating curve.

The burner is still adding heat, so the explanation cannot be that heating stopped.

items.prompt: An atom has atomic number 16 and mass number 34. Which statement about this atom is correct?
options: It has 18 neutrons, and a neutral atom of it has 16 electrons.
It has 34 protons, because the mass number counts the protons.
It has 16 neutrons, because neutrons always equal the protons.
It is a different element from an atom with 16 protons and 16 neutrons.
why: The mass number counts protons and neutrons. Protons equal the atomic number, 16.
Neutron number can differ from proton number. Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 34 − 16 = 18.
Both atoms have 16 protons, so both are the same element. Atoms of one element with different neutron counts are isotopes.
items.explain:
Protons = atomic number = 16. Neutrons = 34 − 16 = 18. A neutral atom has as many electrons as protons: 16.

An atom with 16 protons and 16 neutrons is the same element (sulfur); the two are isotopes, because only the proton count names the element.

items.prompt: Which two are chemical changes? Select two answers.
options: Wood burning to ash in a campfire
An ice cube melting in a glass
Sugar dissolving in hot coffee
An iron nail rusting in the rain
Water boiling in a kettle
why: Melting changes only the state. The melted ice is still water, so it is a physical change.
Dissolved sugar is still sugar; you could recover it by evaporating the coffee. Dissolving is a physical change.
Boiling turns liquid water into water vapor, which is still water. A change of state is physical.
items.explain:
Chemical changes make new substances. Burning wood produces ash, carbon dioxide, and water vapor and gives off heat and light. Rusting makes iron oxide, a new reddish-brown substance.

Melting, dissolving, and boiling leave the substance the same, so they are physical changes.

Hydrogen peroxide slowly breaks down into water and oxygen gas. Choose the coefficients that balance the equation using the smallest whole numbers. (A coefficient of 1 is shown here, although it is usually left unwritten.)

{{0}} H2O2 → {{1}} H2O + {{2}} O2

why: One H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> has 2 O atoms, but 2H<sub>2</sub>O + O<sub>2</sub> has 4. You need 2H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>.
3H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> has 6 H atoms, but 2H<sub>2</sub>O has only 4.
4H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> balances only with 4H<sub>2</sub>O and 2O<sub>2</sub>, which is not the smallest set of whole numbers.
One H<sub>2</sub>O has 2 H atoms, but 2H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> has 4.
3H<sub>2</sub>O has 6 H atoms, but 2H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> has only 4.
4H<sub>2</sub>O has 8 H atoms, twice the 4 in 2H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>.
2O<sub>2</sub> adds 4 O atoms; with 2H<sub>2</sub>O that makes 6 O on the right, but the left has only 4.
3O<sub>2</sub> adds 6 O atoms, far more than the left side has.
4O<sub>2</sub> adds 8 O atoms, far more than the left side has.

items.explain:
Count: left H 2, O 2; right H 2, O 1 + 2 = 3.

Try 2H2O2: left H 4, O 4. Then 2H2O gives H 4 and O 2, and O2 adds 2 more O: right O = 4.

Check: H 4 = 4; O 4 = 4. 2H2O2 → 2H2O + O2.

Leaving every coefficient at 1 gives 2 O on the left and 3 on the right.

items.prompt: A classmate claims that Setup A shows that mass is destroyed when a tablet fizzes. Which evidence from the experiment best shows that this claim is wrong?
options: In Setup B, the total mass stayed the same even though the tablet fizzed.
In Setup A, the total mass went down by 0.55 g after the tablet fizzed.
The water and tablet in Setup B weighed more in total than those in Setup A.
In Setup B, the balloon inflated while the tablet was fizzing in the water.
why: This is the result the classmate is using as evidence. A drop in mass in an open cup does not show the mass was destroyed; it fits gas escaping too.
The starting masses differ only because the containers differ. That difference says nothing about whether mass is conserved during the reaction.
The inflating balloon shows that a gas formed, but by itself it does not show that the total mass was kept. The unchanged balance reading in Setup B does.
items.explain:
In the closed Setup B, the same reaction happened (the tablet fizzed and the balloon filled with gas), yet the total mass stayed at 120.30 g. That shows the mass was not destroyed; in Setup A it simply left the open cup as carbon dioxide gas (105.20 − 104.65 = 0.55 g).

The inflating balloon is tempting, but it only shows a gas formed. The unchanged mass is what refutes the claim.

items.prompt: An empty graduated cylinder has a mass of 42.0 g. A student pours in 25.0 mL of an unknown liquid. The cylinder and liquid together now have a mass of 62.0 g. What is the density of the liquid?

mistakes.why: You divided the total mass, 62.0 g, by the volume. That includes the cylinder. The liquid's mass is 62.0 − 42.0 = 20.0 g.
You divided the volume by the mass (25.0 ÷ 20.0). Density is mass divided by volume.
You divided the empty cylinder's mass by the volume. Use the liquid's mass: 62.0 − 42.0 = 20.0 g.

items.explain:
Mass of liquid = 62.0 g − 42.0 g = 20.0 g.

Density = 20.0 g ÷ 25.0 mL = 0.80 g/mL.

Dividing 62.0 by 25.0 (2.48) includes the cylinder's mass. Since 0.80 < 1.00, this liquid would float on water.

items.prompt: A student makes a saturated solution of potassium chlorate in 100 g of water at 60 °C. She then cools it to 20 °C. About how many grams of potassium chlorate come out of the solution as crystals?
options: 7 g
why: 7 g is the amount that can stay dissolved at 20 °C. The crystals are what is above that limit: 24 − 7.
24 g is the total dissolved at 60 °C. Cooling does not force all of it out; 7 g can still stay dissolved at 20 °C.
You added the two solubilities (24 + 7). Crystals are the difference: what was dissolved minus what can stay dissolved.
items.explain:
A saturated solution at 60 °C holds the limit: 24 g per 100 g of water.

At 20 °C, only 7 g can stay dissolved.

Crystals = 24 g − 7 g = 17 g.

Because the solution was saturated, the amount dissolved equals the 60 °C limit, so subtracting the two solubilities is correct here.

items.prompt: Over several years of acid rain, the pH of a mountain lake dropped from 7 to 5. Which statement correctly describes the change in the lake?
options: The lake became 100 times more acidic than it was before.
The lake became 2 times more acidic than it was before.
The lake became 20 times more acidic than it was before.
The lake became less acidic, because its pH value went down.
why: 2 is the difference in pH units. Each unit is a factor of 10, so 2 units means 10 × 10.
You multiplied the difference by 10. The factors of 10 multiply together: 10 × 10 = 100.
A lower pH means more acidic, not less. pH 5 is more acidic than pH 7.
items.explain:
The pH fell by 7 − 5 = 2 units. Each unit is a factor of 10, so the lake became 10 × 10 = 100 times more acidic. It went from neutral (7) to acidic (5).

"20 times" is the most tempting wrong answer; it multiplies the difference by 10 instead of multiplying the 10s together.

items.prompt: On a hot, humid day, drops of water form on the outside of a glass of iced tea. Which statement best explains where the drops come from?
options: Water vapor in the air loses energy against the cold glass and condenses into liquid.
Iced tea seeps out through tiny holes in the glass and collects on its outside surface.
The cold glass makes oxygen and hydrogen in the air react to form brand-new water.
Ice inside the glass melts, passes through the glass as a gas, and then freezes outside.
why: Glass does not let liquid through, and the drops form even on a glass of plain ice water. They come from the air, not the tea.
No chemical reaction is needed. The water is already in the air as vapor; cooling it only changes its state.
Water cannot pass through glass, and the drops on the outside are liquid, not ice. The water comes from vapor in the air.
items.explain:
Humid air contains water vapor. When vapor particles touch the cold glass, they lose energy, slow down, and come together as liquid. That phase change, gas to liquid, is condensation.

The drops are not tea leaking out; they form on any cold surface in humid air.

items.prompt: Potassium (atomic number 19) is in Group 1 of the periodic table with sodium. Calcium (atomic number 20) is next to potassium in the same row. A potassium atom has mass number 41. Which statement about this atom is correct?
options: It has 22 neutrons, and it reacts with water much as sodium does.
It has 41 protons, and it reacts with water much as sodium does.
It has 22 neutrons, and it behaves most like calcium, its neighbor.
It has 19 neutrons, and it behaves most like calcium, its neighbor.
why: 41 is the mass number, which counts protons and neutrons. Protons equal the atomic number, 19.
The neutron count is right (41 − 19 = 22), but elements in the same row do not share properties. Potassium shares a column with sodium, so it behaves like sodium.
Neutrons are 41 − 19 = 22, not 19, and potassium behaves like sodium (same group), not calcium (same row).
items.explain:
Neutrons = 41 − 19 = 22. Potassium is in the same group as sodium, so it has the same number of outer electrons and reacts with water in a similar way.

Calcium is tempting because it is right next to potassium, but properties are shared down a column, not across a row.

items.prompt: Which two are physical changes? Select two answers.
options: Chocolate melting in a warm car
Bread browning in a toaster
Natural gas burning on a stove
Cutting a sheet of aluminum foil
A copper roof turning green over many years
why: Browning toast forms new substances with a new color, smell, and taste. That is a chemical change.
Burning natural gas makes carbon dioxide and water and gives off heat and light. New substances mean a chemical change.
The green coating is a new compound that forms when copper reacts with substances in the air. A color change from a new substance is chemical.
items.explain:
Physical changes leave the substance the same. Melted chocolate is still chocolate, and cut foil is still aluminum.

Toasting bread, burning natural gas, and the green coating on copper all make new substances, so they are chemical changes.

{{0}} KClO3 → {{1}} KCl + {{2}} O2

why: One KClO<sub>3</sub> has 3 O atoms, an odd number; O<sub>2</sub> supplies oxygen in pairs, so you need 2KClO<sub>3</sub> (6 O).
3KClO<sub>3</sub> has 9 O atoms, an odd number that O<sub>2</sub> pairs cannot match.
4KClO<sub>3</sub> balances only with 4KCl and 6O<sub>2</sub>, which is not the smallest set of whole numbers.
One KCl has 1 K atom, but 2KClO<sub>3</sub> has 2.
3KCl has 3 K atoms, but 2KClO<sub>3</sub> has only 2.
4KCl has 4 K atoms, twice the 2 in 2KClO<sub>3</sub>.
One O<sub>2</sub> has 2 O atoms, but 2KClO<sub>3</sub> has 6.
2O<sub>2</sub> has 4 O atoms, but 2KClO<sub>3</sub> has 6.
4O<sub>2</sub> has 8 O atoms, but 2KClO<sub>3</sub> has only 6.

items.explain:
Count: left K 1, Cl 1, O 3; right K 1, Cl 1, O 2.

Oxygen is 3 on the left and 2 on the right. The least common multiple is 6: write 2KClO3 (2 × 3 = 6) and 3O2 (3 × 2 = 6).

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the student's observations and data?
options: A chemical change occurred, and the total mass of the substances stayed the same.
No reaction occurred, because the total mass of the flask did not change at all.
Only a physical change occurred, because no gas bubbles were produced by mixing.
Mass was gained when the solid formed, but the amount was too small to measure.
why: Mass stays the same in every reaction in a sealed container, so an unchanged mass does not mean nothing happened. The new white solid shows a reaction did occur.
Gas is only one sign of a chemical change. A new solid forming when two liquids are mixed (a precipitate) is also evidence of a new substance.
Mass is never gained or lost in a chemical reaction. The balance showed exactly the same mass, which is what conservation of mass predicts.
items.explain:
A cloudy white solid formed when two clear solutions mixed. A new solid (a precipitate) is evidence of a chemical change. The sealed flask weighed 150.40 g before and after, so the total mass was conserved.

The tempting wrong answer says no reaction occurred because the mass did not change, but conservation of mass means the mass stays the same even when a reaction happens.

items.prompt: An empty beaker has a mass of 50.0 g. A cook pours 40.0 mL of corn syrup into it. The beaker and syrup together now have a mass of 105.2 g. What is the density of the corn syrup? Round to the nearest hundredth.

mistakes.why: You divided the total mass, 105.2 g, by the volume. That includes the beaker. The syrup's mass is 105.2 − 50.0 = 55.2 g.
You divided the volume by the mass (40.0 ÷ 55.2). Density is mass divided by volume.
You divided the empty beaker's mass by the volume. Use the syrup's mass: 105.2 − 50.0 = 55.2 g.

items.explain:
Mass of syrup = 105.2 g − 50.0 g = 55.2 g.

Density = 55.2 g ÷ 40.0 mL = 1.38 g/mL.

Dividing 105.2 by 40.0 (2.63) includes the beaker's mass. Since 1.38 > 1.00, corn syrup sinks below water.

66 g is the total dissolved at 80 °C. Cooling does not force all of it out; 46 g can still stay dissolved at 40 °C.
You added the two solubilities (66 + 46). Crystals are the difference: what was dissolved minus what can stay dissolved.
items.explain:
A saturated solution at 80 °C holds the limit: 66 g per 100 g of water.

At 40 °C, only 46 g can stay dissolved.

Crystals = 66 g − 46 g = 20 g.

Because the solution was saturated, the amount dissolved equals the 80 °C limit, so subtracting the two solubilities is correct here.

items.prompt: A gardener's soil has a pH of 5. She mixes in lime, which is a base. A week later, the soil's pH is 6. Which statement correctly describes the soil now?
options: It is 10 times less acidic than before, but it is still slightly acidic.
It is 10 times more acidic than before, because its pH number went up.
It is now neutral, because the base neutralized all of the acid in it.
It is 2 times less acidic than before, because its pH went up by 1 unit.
why: A higher pH means less acidic. Adding a base moves the pH up toward 7, which lowers the acidity.
Neutral is pH 7. At pH 6 the soil is still slightly acidic; the lime has only partly neutralized the acid.
A 1-unit change is a factor of 10, not 2. Each pH unit multiplies or divides the acidity by 10.
items.explain:
The pH rose from 5 to 6, one unit, so the soil is 10 times less acidic. Because 6 is still below 7, the soil is still slightly acidic. The base partly neutralized the acid.

Calling the soil neutral is tempting, but neutral is exactly pH 7.

vocab.def: Anything that has mass and takes up space.
vocab.example: Air, water, and a rock are all matter.

vocab.def: The smallest unit of an element that still has that element's properties; made of protons, neutrons, and electrons.
The number of protons in an atom; it decides which element the atom is.
vocab.example: Oxygen's atomic number is 8, so every oxygen atom has 8 protons.

vocab.def: The total number of protons and neutrons in an atom's nucleus.
vocab.example: Carbon-14 has 6 protons and 8 neutrons, so its mass number is 14.

vocab.def: A pure substance made of only one kind of atom.
A substance made of two or more elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio.
vocab.example: Water, H<sub>2</sub>O, always has two hydrogen atoms for every oxygen atom.

vocab.def: Two or more substances combined without bonding; they can be separated by physical means.
vocab.example: Sand and iron filings can be separated with a magnet.

vocab.def: A change that produces one or more new substances.
A change in size, shape, or state that does not make a new substance.
A number placed in front of a formula in a chemical equation to show how many units of it react or form.
In a chemical reaction, matter is neither created nor destroyed, so the mass of the reactants equals the mass of the products.
vocab.example: 10 g of reactants always make 10 g of products.

vocab.def: The amount of mass in a given volume; density = mass ÷ volume.
vocab.example: A 20 g object with a volume of 10 mL has a density of 2 g/mL.

vocab.def: The greatest amount of a solute that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent at a given temperature.
vocab.example: About 36 g of table salt can dissolve in 100 g of water at 20 °C.

vocab.def: The amount of solute in a given amount of solution.
vocab.example: 5 g of sugar in 1 L of tea is a concentration of 5 g/L.

vocab.def: A scale from 0 to 14 that measures how acidic or basic a solution is; below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral, above 7 is basic.
vocab.example: Vinegar has a pH of about 3, so it is an acid.

notes:
Study Notes: Chemistry

States of Matter

Solid: fixed shape and volume. Liquid: fixed volume. Gas: neither.
Add heat: melt, evaporate/boil, sublimate. Remove heat: freeze, condense.
Temperature stays flat during a phase change (the flat parts of a heating curve: lower = melting/freezing, higher = boiling/condensing).

The Atom

Atomic number = protons
Mass number = protons + neutrons
Neutrons = mass # − atomic #
Neutral atom: electrons = protons
Isotopes: same protons, different neutrons. Ion: gained or lost electrons.

Periodic table: columns = groups (similar properties); rows = periods. Metals left, nonmetals right, noble gases far right (Group 18).

Element / Compound / Mixture

Element: one kind of atom (Fe, O2).
Compound: bonded, fixed ratio (H2O, NaCl).
Mixture: not bonded, separable (salt water, air).

Changes

Physical: same substance (melt, cut, dissolve).
Chemical: new substance. Clues: gas, color change, heat/light, new solid.

Balancing Equations

  1. Count atoms on each side.
  2. Change coefficients only, never subscripts.
  3. Coefficient × subscript = atoms (3H2O: 6 H, 3 O).
  4. Recount; use smallest whole numbers.

Conservation of mass: mass of reactants = mass of products. Open container + gas made = mass seems to drop.

Formulas

Density = mass ÷ volume (water = 1.00 g/mL)
Displacement volume = final − starting level
Concentration (g/L) = g solute ÷ L solution (mL ÷ 1,000 = L)
Diluting: same grams of solute ÷ new total volume

TypeAcid (sour; blue litmus turns red)Neutral (pure water)Base (bitter, slippery; red litmus turns blue)
ExamplesLemon juice 2, vinegar 3Water 7Baking soda 9, ammonia 11

pH rule: 1 unit = 10 times; 2 units = 100 times; 3 units = 1,000 times. Solubility: most solids dissolve more in warm water; gases dissolve more in cold. Cooling a solution below its limit makes crystals: amount out = amount dissolved − new limit.
